# Introduction

The transgene assay tells us *whether* a cell carries the lentiviral cassette. This report asks a
harder question: **where in the genome did it integrate**, and can that be used as a clone label.

The idea rests on a leak in the vector. Transcription of the cassette is supposed to terminate at the
polyadenylation site in the 3′ LTR's R region, at contig 3152. Termination is not perfect, and a
minority of transcripts read through to the end of the provirus and on into the flanking host DNA.
Such a molecule aligns to the reporter contig as far as its last base and then stops matching, so the
aligner soft-clips the remainder — and that clipped tail is host sequence that names the integration
locus. Because the read still carries its 10x cell barcode and UMI, the locus comes attached to a
**cell**.

## Why the junction is at exactly one position

Integration chemistry fixes it. Reverse transcription makes a blunt double-stranded DNA whose plus
strand ends `…TGGAAAATCTCTAGCA`**`GT`**. Integrase then performs 3′ processing: it removes that
terminal `GT`, leaving a recessed 3′-OH on a `CA`, and it is that `CA` which attacks the host DNA in
the strand-transfer step.

```
…host host host │ CA ──────── provirus ──────── CA │ host host host…
                  ↑                                 ↑
            processed end                      processed end
```

The reporter contig ends `…TCTCTAG`**`CA`** — exactly that processed terminus. So **contig position
3236 is the integration junction itself**, and a clip anchored anywhere else cannot be one. That is a
statement about enzymology rather than a tuning parameter, which is why it is the first filter
applied and why it costs no sensitivity.

It also does the heavy lifting against artefacts, as the next section shows.

# How these tables were produced

This report does no site calling of its own. It reads five CSVs written by a batch job and plots them,
so that re-rendering is cheap and the calling is reproducible independently of the report.

## The pipeline

```
data/cellranger_<tube>/sample_alignments.bam        8 tubes, ~55 GB each
        │
        │  1. EXTRACT   src/R/integration-sites.R :: read_junction_clips(), classify_clips()
        │     Rsamtools reads a 87-base window of one contig per tube (seconds, despite the
        │     BAM size), keeps reads whose anchor ends exactly at the junction, and splits the
        │     soft-clipped tails into the discovery and assignment tiers.
        ▼
   work/discovery.fa  work/assign.fa  work/five_prime.fa
        │
        │  2. ALIGN (genome)   bwa mem -k 16 -T 20. The seed is shortened because a 25-48
        │     base query will not seed at the default 19 -- and -T is set explicitly because
        │     the default of 30 silently discarded every clip below 30 bp, 244 of them, while
        │     min_discovery advertised 25.
        ▼
   work/discovery.sam  work/five_prime.sam
        │
        │  3. GENOMIC   read_genomic_clips()
        │     The second, independent read of the same junctions: reads STAR placed on the
        │     HOST genome with the vector soft-clipped, which stage 1 cannot see because it
        │     only ever reads one window of one contig. The coordinate is already resolved at
        │     MAPQ 255 behind 120-140 bases of host, so no alignment follows. A streaming pass
        │     over every alignment in each BAM, one core per tube, cached per tube.
        ▼
   work/genomic_<tube>.csv                          cached per tube; schema declared on read back,
        │                                            because the wild-type tubes cache zero rows
        │
        │  3b. GENOMIC DECOY (optional)   genomic_decoy_rate()
        │     The same scan with the terminus permuted to the same base composition, which bounds
        │     this channel's false-positive rate the way the decoy flanks bound assignment's. Costs
        │     what stage 3 costs, so it is opt-in and takes a chromosome argument.
        ▼
   genomic_decoy_rate.csv
        │
        │  4. SITES     call_sites(), label_sites(), summarise_sites(), write_site_flanks()
        │     GenomicRanges clusters BOTH channels' placements into sites together -- the
        │     genome-mapped reads call sites on their own, and four of the fifteen exist only
        │     because of them -- the cell and UMI floor is applied, label_sites() pins each
        │     locus to its IS number from metadata/integration_site_registry.csv, rtracklayer
        │     annotates the host gene, the flanks are cut, and 100 DECOY flanks from random
        │     matched positions go into the same file to measure the error rate.
        ▼
   work/site_flanks.fa                              12 real flanks + 100 decoys
        │
        │  5. ASSIGN    assign_clips_exact(), genomic_site_hits(), decoy_error_rate(),
        │     summarise_cells(), update_site_counts(), channel_capture_recapture(),
        │     tsd_check(), rescue_orphan_junctions(), junction_coverage()
        │     No aligner. The clip must match a flank at the junction base exactly, forward or
        │     reverse-complemented, within the mismatch budget. The genome-mapped reads then
        │     rejoin as CELL evidence rather than only as discovery: they already carry their
        │     coordinate, so genomic_site_hits() returns each to the site it was clustered
        │     into. Leaving them out halved the clone sizes of the largest sites.
        ▼
   output/objects/integration-sites/*.csv           what this report reads
```

bwa used to run a second time here, against the flanks. It was removed: MAPQ against a handful of
short sequences is near-meaningless and was already being ignored, `-a` had to be passed to stop its
ranking discarding true hits, and `-T 12` silently enforced a 12 bp floor while `min_assign`
advertised 8 — 169 reads written and dropped with no error, the same failure as `-T 30` one tier up.
**That `-T 12` problem is resolved by removal, not by a fix:** there is no aligner in this tier any
more, so the flag gates nothing and cannot be reintroduced by changing a threshold. It is recorded
here so nobody reopens it looking for the setting that corrects it.
What remained once those were stripped away was a positional test, which is exact, deterministic and
runs in seconds.

## Files

| file | role |
|---|---|
| [`src/R/integration-sites.R`](../../src/R/integration-sites.R) | all the logic, as functions. Attaches no packages, so it can be `source()`d and stepped through. Every threshold is in `IS_DEFAULTS` at the top. |
| [`scripts/R/call-integration-sites.R`](../../scripts/R/call-integration-sites.R) | driver with four entry points — `extract`, `genomic`, `sites`, `assign` — split where bwa has to run between them, and where the genomic scan has to be restartable on its own |
| [`scripts/slurm/analysis/integration-sites.sh`](../../scripts/slurm/analysis/integration-sites.sh) | the batch job, five stages. The genomic scan dominates: ~105 min for eight BAMs forked one core per tube, against ~14 h in series. Everything else is minutes. |
| [`scripts/slurm/analysis/integration-sites-decoy.sh`](../../scripts/slurm/analysis/integration-sites-decoy.sh) | the genome-mapped channel's error bound: the same scan with the terminus permuted to the same base composition. Its own job, ~1 h 50 m, because a control must not sit on the critical path. Takes an optional chromosome |
| [`scripts/slurm/setup/bwa-index.sh`](../../scripts/slurm/setup/bwa-index.sh) | builds the bwa index once, ~50 min |

Both jobs run on the `short` partition and **not** the `_el9` ones: renv keys its library path on the
OS release, so on a Rocky 9 node it finds no library and the first `library()` call fails.

## Inputs

| input | where from |
|---|---|
| `data/cellranger_<tube>/sample_alignments.bam` | `scripts/slurm/cellranger/cellranger-multi.sh`, linked into `data/` so the provenance catalogue sees it |
| `$CR_REF/bwa/genome.*` | the mouse genome **plus the reporter contig**, indexed. The contig is included deliberately: a clip landing back on the vector is then recognisable rather than quietly unmapped. |
| `$CR_REF/genes/genes.gtf.gz` | GRCm39 / GENCODE vM33, for the host-gene annotation |
| `metadata/cellranger/libraries.csv` | the list of tubes to process |
| [`metadata/integration_site_registry.csv`](../../metadata/integration_site_registry.csv) | pins each `IS` label to its locus, so a label means the same site across runs. Written by `label_sites()`; tracked, because `output/` is not. See *Site labels are pinned, not ranked* below. |

## Outputs

| file | rows | one row per |
|---|---|---|
| `integration_sites.csv` | 15 | **site**: position, strand, host gene, reads/cells/UMIs, and cells per tube |
| `cell_site_assignments.csv` | ~1,200 | **cell × site**: the table that joins onto Seurat metadata and turns a locus into a clone label. Carries `channels`, `reads_three`, `reads_genomic`, `umis_three` and `umis_genomic` per cell, so the per-site overlap between the two channels stays recoverable — collapsing it to one label would destroy the channel-overlap analysis without a re-run. The UMI columns are not a convenience: the overlap has to be counted in molecules, and counting it in reads gets the answer wrong by a factor of three. |
| `clip_waterfall.csv` | 33 | tube × filter class — every clip counted once, under the first reason it met |
| `anchor_ends.csv` | 811 | tube × anchor position × clip length — the coverage view below |
| `site_calling_summary.csv` | 7 | what each tier contributed |
| `decoy_error_rate.csv` | 5 | clip-length band × the decoy hit rate, and ε scaled to the real flanks |
| `tsd_check.csv` | 8 | 5′ cluster: signed Δ, the duplicated span, whether reads contain it, strand agreement |
| `orphan_rescue.csv` | 4 | orphan 5′ junction tested at the one position its partner must occupy, with the denominator |
| `junction_coverage.csv` | — | site × channel × offset: the pile-up figure |
| `genomic_decoy_rate.csv` | 8 | tube: real against decoy hits for the genome-mapped channel, from the scrambled-terminus run. Region-tagged when restricted to one chromosome, so a narrow probe cannot overwrite a genome-wide measurement |
| `clip_floor_curve.csv` | ~50 | clip length: what a clip of that length matches, real sites and decoy flanks, under both the exact and budgeted rules. **The measurement that sets `min_assign` and `exact_below`** |
| `repertoire_completeness.csv` | 1 | the assumption-free floor and the detection-corrected share of the mCherry⁺ population, with the number of sites whose detection had to be imputed |
| `unassigned_molecules.csv` | 4 | what becomes of junction molecules matching no called site: below the floor, unplaceable, or at a locus that failed the cell floor |
| `ambient_rate.csv` | 8 | tube: junction-bearing barcodes that are and are not called cells, per-cell against per-empty-droplet |
| `work/called_barcodes.csv.gz` | ~161,000 | Cell Ranger's called barcodes, captured with the run so every cell count is reproducible from the outputs alone |
| `detection_model.csv` | 15 | site: per-cell detection rate from a zero-truncated Poisson on molecule counts, the detection-corrected clone size with a bootstrap interval, and the observed-against-fitted check. `NA` where the truncated mean is too close to 1 to fit — that is the estimator declining, not a gap |
| `clip_table.csv.gz` | ~1,800 | **molecule**: one row per tube + barcode + UMI with **no floor**, its longest clip, and how many called sites and decoy flanks that clip matches. The table every floor and detection question is answered from |
| `clip_matches.csv.gz` | ~9,000 | clip × flank × orientation with the mismatch count, for anything the molecule view collapses away |
| `channel_capture_recapture.csv` | 15 | site: cells seen by each channel, their overlap, Chapman's estimator — **and the molecule-model expectation that stops it being read as a clone size** |

## Re-running it

```bash
sbatch scripts/slurm/setup/bwa-index.sh          # once, if the reference changes
sbatch scripts/slurm/analysis/integration-sites.sh
```

To change a threshold, edit `IS_DEFAULTS` in `src/R/integration-sites.R` — the job file holds no
analysis parameters of its own, so the two cannot disagree. To work interactively instead:

```r
source("src/R/integration-sites.R")
clips <- read_junction_clips("data/cellranger_Rx_4/sample_alignments.bam", "Rx_4")
table(classify_clips(clips)$class)

# the genome-mapped channel, restricted to a window so it returns in seconds rather than ~105 min
read_genomic_clips("data/cellranger_Rx_4/sample_alignments.bam", "Rx_4",
                   region = GenomicRanges::GRanges("chr9", IRanges::IRanges(53079416, 53080416)))
```

Two parameters in `IS_DEFAULTS` are measurements rather than preferences, and should not be adjusted
without redoing the measurement. `min_assign = 10` is where the decoy flanks stop returning hits.
`absorb_window = 2` is **mandatory**: the provirus's terminal base is absorbed into the host
alignment whenever it matches the host's first base, and without the tolerance the boundary test
returns zero hits at a site known to be there — a failure that presents as "the channel doesn't
work" rather than as a bug.

The thresholds used for the tables in this report:

```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)
library(DT)
library(targets)

source("src/R/integration-sites.R")   # IS_DEFAULTS: the thresholds the pipeline actually used

sites_dir <- "output/objects/integration-sites"
stopifnot(dir.exists(sites_dir))

anchor_ends <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "anchor_ends.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
waterfall   <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "clip_waterfall.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sites       <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "integration_sites.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
assign      <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "cell_site_assignments.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
summary_tbl <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "site_calling_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
tsd         <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "tsd_check.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
coverage    <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "junction_coverage.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# One factor with every site as a level, so a clone keeps the same colour in every panel even where
# it has no cells. As a bare character it would be re-levelled per panel and the colours would shift.
assign$site_id <- factor(assign$site_id, levels = sites$site_id)

# Clone colours. These are nominal categories with no order, so a sampled continuous ramp (viridis,
# turbo) is the wrong tool: neighbouring clones come out as neighbouring hues. glasbey is built by
# maximising distance in CIELAB, and measurably wins here - the closest pair of colours is 67 dE
# apart against 28 for the project's .discrete_colours() at n = 9 and 24 for turbo. Its first entry
# is black, dropped so no clone is confused with text or an axis.
#
# The trade-off, stated because it is real: glasbey is not optimised for colour vision deficiency
# (closest pair under deuteranopia ~9 dE). Okabe-Ito and Tol muted do better there (~17) but are far
# worse for normal vision (~26 and ~23), and their low chroma washes out at this point size. If a
# reader needs CVD-safe output, swap this one line.
# Keyed on the site LABEL, not on its position in the table. The labels are pinned to loci by the
# registry, but the table is sorted by size, so keying the palette on position would move every
# clone's colour the moment one changed rank - the same failure the registry fixed for the labels,
# and harder to notice in a figure. Sorted ids mean IS01 keeps its colour and a new site appends.
pal_ids      <- sort(levels(assign$site_id))
site_palette <- stats::setNames(as.character(pals::glasbey(length(pal_ids) + 1))[-1], pal_ids)

# Taken from the pipeline rather than restated, so the figures cannot drift from the run.
JUNCTION <- IS_DEFAULTS$junction
MIN_DISC <- IS_DEFAULTS$min_discovery
MIN_ASSIGN <- IS_DEFAULTS$min_assign
CLEAVAGE <- 3152L   # measured from the polyA clips; see reference_additions/README.md

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
```

```{r is-defaults}
dplyr::tibble(parameter = names(IS_DEFAULTS),
              value     = vapply(IS_DEFAULTS, as.character, character(1))) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 12))
```


# The coverage view

This is the figure that decides whether the whole approach is viable: do enough reads actually reach
the junction? Each soft-clipped read is placed at the position where its anchor stops matching the
contig, and coloured by whether its clipped tail is adenine.

```{r anchor-ends, fig.height=6}
ends_by_tube <- anchor_ends %>%
  dplyr::group_by(tube, anchor_end, polya) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(reads = sum(reads), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(ends_by_tube, aes(anchor_end, reads, fill = polya)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = CLEAVAGE, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = JUNCTION, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ tube, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey70", `FALSE` = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "polyA tail", `FALSE` = "non-polyA")) +
  labs(x = "contig position where the anchor stops matching",
       y = "reads", fill = NULL,
       title = "Two populations of soft-clipped reads",
       subtitle = sprintf("dashed grey = polyA cleavage site (%d); dashed red = integration junction (%d)",
                          CLEAVAGE, JUNCTION))
```

Two piles, and they mean completely different things.

The pile at the **cleavage site** is the transcript's own polyA tail: the read reaches the end of the
mRNA and clips the A's. It says nothing about integration. The pile at the **junction** is the
read-through population, and its clips are host sequence.

```{r two-populations}
ends_by_tube %>%
  dplyr::mutate(pile = dplyr::case_when(
    anchor_end >= CLEAVAGE - 8 & anchor_end <= CLEAVAGE ~ "cleavage site (3144–3152)",
    anchor_end == JUNCTION                              ~ "junction (3236)",
    TRUE                                                ~ "elsewhere")) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(pile, polya) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(reads = sum(reads), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = polya, values_from = reads, values_fill = 0,
                     names_prefix = "polya_") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(total = polya_TRUE + polya_FALSE,
                pct_polya = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * polya_TRUE / total)) %>%
  dplyr::select(pile, total, polya = polya_TRUE, non_polya = polya_FALSE, pct_polya) %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

The separation is what makes the anchor-position filter worth so much. The non-polyA minority of the
cleavage-site pile is the dangerous part: those reads have good MAPQ, real barcodes and real UMIs, so
they would align somewhere in 2.7 Gb and be counted as sites. Nothing downstream would catch them —
they look exactly like evidence. Requiring the anchor to end at 3236 removes them before the aligner
ever sees them.


# The filter waterfall

```{r waterfall}
# the order classify_clips() applies them in: each clip is counted once, under the first reason it
# met, so the columns sum to every soft-clipped read in the scan window
class_order <- c("anchor not at the junction", "vector (5' LTR to psi)", "polyA tail",
                 "no cell barcode or UMI", "clip too short to place", "assign", "discovery")

waterfall %>%
  dplyr::mutate(class = factor(class, levels = class_order)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(class) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = tube, values_from = reads, values_fill = 0) %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", scrollX = TRUE))
```

Three of those discards deserve comment.

**Vector (5′ LTR → ψ).** The plasmid's two LTRs are byte-identical over all 181 bases, and the contig
deliberately keeps only one copy so that reads landing in the LTR do not multi-map. The side effect is
that a molecule spanning the **5′** LTR's junction with ψ presents a left arm matching the contig's 3′
terminus perfectly — so it is placed at 3236, with MAPQ 255, and clips into vector sequence. It is
structurally indistinguishable from a host junction. No MAPQ or coverage filter sees it, because the
anchor genuinely *is* a unique alignment; only the sequence of the clip gives it away. This filter is
load-bearing, not cosmetic.

**polyA.** A small number of polyA clips occur at the junction too, from internal priming.

**Clip too short to place.** Discussed next.


# Clip length: how much host sequence is enough

The clip is host genome, so its length is exactly how much flanking sequence the read delivered. Too
short and it cannot be placed uniquely in a 2.7 Gb genome; the information-theoretic floor is about 16
bases, and in practice mismatches and repeats push the usable threshold higher.

### Four numbers, three tiers — which is which

Three different length floors are live in this analysis and a fourth is historical. They are not
alternatives and carrying one into another tier is the single most expensive mistake this pipeline
has made, twice: `-T 30` voided a 25 bp floor and `-T 12` voided an 8 bp one, both silently. Each
number belongs to a tier, and the tier is what sets it, because the prior odds differ by six orders
of magnitude.

| number | tier | what is being searched | why that number |
|---|---|---|---|
| **25 bp** `min_discovery` | 3′ discovery | **2.7 Gb** of genome, no prior | long enough for bwa to place uniquely; 86 of 974 clips still land at MAPQ 0 |
| **13 bp** `min_genomic` | genome-mapped channel | **one position** in a read already placed at MAPQ 255 | an exact match to the provirus terminus, as a confirmation on a read the aligner has already located — not a placement |
| **6 bp** `min_assign` | assignment | **~3.6 kb** of called flanks, and one accepted offset in each | measured per base: the 100 decoy flanks are clean from 6 bp up under exact matching, dirty below |
| **15 bp** `exact_below` | assignment | — | not a length floor but its companion: beneath it a clip must match **exactly**, because the `L %/% 10` budget allows one mismatch and that is what the decoys catch |
| ~~8 bp~~, ~~10 bp~~ | — | — | superseded, each for a different reason. 8 came from the wild-type tubes being empty, which bounds cross-tube hopping and not within-tube chance matching — the wrong instrument. 10 came from the right instrument read at the wrong resolution: decoy hits in coarse bands with a mismatch allowed |

**Do not carry 6 bp into discovery.** A 6 bp query matches somewhere in 2.7 Gb roughly every 4 kb. It
is safe for assignment only because assignment is not a search: the flank set is ~3.6 kb, the clip
must land on one exact offset, and the decoys measure what that costs. 13 bp is not a discovery floor
either — it is a confirmation on a read whose coordinate came from 120–140 bases of host.

### Where the assignment floor is, and how it was measured

`min_assign` is **6**, with exact matching required beneath 15 bases. Both numbers come from one
measurement, computed each run rather than quoted: `clip_table.csv.gz` carries every clip against
every flank at every mismatch count with **no floor**, so the question can be asked one base at a
time. The 100 decoy flanks are the instrument — a decoy has no junction, so a decoy match at a given
length *is* the chance rate at that length — and decoys can be cut at will, so there is no
sample-size limit.

```{r floor-curve}
readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "clip_floor_curve.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(clip_len <= 20) |>
  dplyr::transmute(`clip length` = clip_len, molecules,
                   `one site, exact` = unique_exact, `>1 site, exact` = ambiguous_exact,
                   `hit a decoy, exact` = decoy_exact,
                   `hit a decoy, with the budget` = decoy_budget,
                   `floor` = ifelse(at_or_above_floor, "in", "out"),
                   `exact required` = ifelse(exact_required, "yes", "no")) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 20, scrollX = TRUE)) |>
  DT::formatStyle("hit a decoy, exact", target = "row",
                  backgroundColor = DT::styleInterval(0, c("#e8f5e9", "#fde8e8")))
```

**Clean from 6 bp up, dirty below.** At 6 bp, 27 molecules match exactly one real site and **none of
the 100 decoys**; at 5 bp one molecule in nine hits a decoy, at 4 bp ten of seventeen do, and at 1–2
bp a clip matches most of the decoy set — the prior-inflation hazard made visible rather than argued.
Read it as a bound: zero hits in 35 × 100 comparisons at 6 bp, not a demonstrated zero.

**The 6 bp row also shows why the two thresholds are one decision.** Under the `L %/% 10` mismatch
budget, **21 of those 35 molecules hit a decoy**. Under exact matching, zero do. A 6-base clip allowed
one mismatch matches almost anything, so lowering the floor without `exact_below` would have been
strictly worse than leaving it at 10.

**What the change cost and bought.** Against the previous rule — floor 10, budget throughout — the
new rule gains **57** three-prime assignments and loses **5**:

| | clip lengths | assignments |
|---|---|---|
| gained, newly above the floor | 6, 7, 8, 9 bp | 25, 20, 4, 8 |
| **lost**, now rejected for carrying a mismatch | 10, 11, 12 bp | 1, 1, 3 |

The five losses are the point rather than a regret: they are assignments that previously rested on a
mismatch at a length where the decoys say a mismatch is unsafe. Net across both channels, with the
called-cell filter applied at the same time, the table moves from 1,213 assignments over 1,186 cells
to **1,222 over 1,195**.

**A second instrument exists and does not decide this.** Because every site belongs to one mouse,
a clip assigned to a site in the *wrong* mouse is a detectable error on real reads. It agrees with
the decoys at the current floor, but it cannot set one — it measures chance matching plus hashtag
error plus doublets, and it has 8% power against a 1% error rate at the band that matters. It needs
the hashtag calls, so it is computed further down, under *Cells carrying more than one site*.

#### How much ambiguity there is to resolve, which bounds everything above

One number sizes the whole question. Across the entire dataset, **25 molecules match more than one
called site exactly** — and every one of them has a clip of 1 or 2 bases. At 6 bp and above, every
molecule that matches a site matches exactly one. There is no ambiguity above 2 bp for any
tie-breaking rule to work on.

That bounds the most attractive idea for breaking the ties, too. Because every site belongs to one
mouse and each cell's hashtag names its mouse, the candidate sites for a cell can be restricted from
all fifteen to the 2–7 in its own mouse (B0301 holds 2, B0304 6, B0303 7). Applied to those 25
molecules it resolves **8** of them to a single site, leaves 13 still ambiguous, and finds no hashtag
call for 4. So it works, it is free, and it operates on eight molecules at clip lengths that should
not be used anyway. Worth knowing before building anything on it.

Its companion instrument, the labelled validation set, is thinner still: 573 cells carry a ≥20 bp
clip and 151 carry a sub-floor clip, but only **27 carry both**. That is enough to catch a gross
disagreement and nothing finer, because sub-floor molecules come one to a cell — all 151 of them, in
151 different cells. **No cell in this data carries two sub-floor molecules**, which also retires the
idea of aggregating several short clips within a cell into one confident call: it has no instances
here. At λ ≈ 0.3–0.7 you do not get two attempts at the same cell. The exception is instructive:
IS05, at 2.63 molecules a cell, is the one site where within-cell replication exists at all.

```{r clip-length}
junction_clips <- anchor_ends %>%
  dplyr::filter(anchor_end == JUNCTION, !polya)

ggplot(junction_clips, aes(clip_len, weight = reads)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = MIN_ASSIGN, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = MIN_DISC, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "clip length (bases of host sequence)", y = "reads",
       title = "How much host sequence the read-through reads deliver",
       subtitle = sprintf("dashed grey = assignment threshold (%d); dashed red = discovery threshold (%d)",
                          MIN_ASSIGN, MIN_DISC))
```

Rather than pick one threshold, the pipeline asks two different questions and gives each its own.

| tier | clip | searched against | asks |
|---|---|---|---|
| discovery | ≥ `r MIN_DISC` bp | the whole genome, 2.7 Gb | is there an integration *anywhere*? |
| assignment | ≥ `r MIN_ASSIGN` bp | the called flanks, a few kb | does this clip match a site *already found*? |

Those are not the same question, and treating them as one is what the old single threshold did.
Discovery must survive 2.7 Gb of alternatives, so it needs a clip long enough to be unique there.
Assignment only has to choose among a handful of known flanks — **and the clip must land on the
junction base exactly**, not merely somewhere in the flank. That positional constraint is the real
discriminator, and it is strong enough that a 10 bp clip is decisive: it has 400 places to land in
each flank and one is accepted. The floor is 10 rather than 8 because that is where the decoy flanks
stop returning hits — 8 and 9 bp return two between them, 10 bp and above return none.

The evidence that this is safe rather than merely generous is the control: 28,010 cells across the
wild-type tubes that never saw the vector. Dropping the threshold from 25 to 10 raises labelled
cells by about two thirds and leaves them at zero.

They are no longer at exactly zero, and the events are worth running down rather than rounding away,
because the UMIs identify what each one is. Four junction-bearing barcodes sit in wild-type tubes —
two in Rx_1 and two in Rx_5 — and the called-cell filter is what separates them:

- **The Rx_5 pair are not cells**, and one of them is **index hopping, demonstrated rather than
  inferred**: the read carries 121 bases of host at MAPQ 255, and its UMI `AGGCGGTTGTGT` appears at
  the same junction base in **Rx_6**, as does its barcode. One molecule from one cell, read out under
  two sample indices. Both Rx_5 barcodes are absent from Cell Ranger's filtered list, so the
  called-cell filter removes them — which is the right outcome and also a check on it: the one
  provable hopping event in the data landed in an empty droplet, not in a cell.
- **One Rx_1 barcode is a called cell**, and it survives. Its 32-base clip carries UMI
  `AGGGGTTACCAG`, which appears in no other tube, and neither does its barcode. A single read with no
  second-index twin is either genuine carry-over of a cell or a chance match; one read cannot
  distinguish them.

So among called cells the cross-tube rate is **1 in 1,222**, and that one event is unexplained rather
than demonstrated. The demonstrable hopping is in the ambient fraction, where it does no harm.
That is what the wild-type tubes were included to supply, and it is a tighter answer than a
percentage.

```{r tier-contribution}
summary_tbl %>% DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 12))
```


# The sites

```{r site-table}
sites %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
                options = list(pageLength = 20, scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  DT::formatStyle("cells", fontWeight = "bold")
```

### What each channel contributes

Fifteen sites, and the two channels do not contribute equally to that list. Run each one's reads
through the same site caller on its own:

Running each channel's reads through the same site caller alone gives 9 sites from the 3′ channel
and 13 from the genome-mapped one — which recovers **every** site the 3′ channel finds, the 3′-only
column being empty, and adds four of its own. That leaves 9 + 4 = 13 against a pooled call of 15, so
the arithmetic needs a third category rather than a sentence. `site_provenance()` records it per site:

```{r called-by}
sites |>
  dplyr::group_by(`called by` = called_by) |>
  dplyr::summarise(sites = dplyr::n(),
                   which = paste(sort(site_id), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sites)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**IS14 and IS15 clear the cell floor only on the two channels' reads summed** — neither channel
reaches `min_cells` at either locus alone. That is legitimate evidence and it is also the weakest
evidence in the set, so they are flagged `pooled_only` in the site table. They are the same two
sites the mini-reference gate holds out for lacking 5′ confirmation, which is not a coincidence:
nothing independent vouches for either. **Exclude them from any repertoire count, diversity
statistic or denominator** until a second line of evidence arrives. Saying "15 sites" without that
caveat overstates what was found; the defensible count is **13**.

The largest addition is not marginal. **IS10, `chr13:5,676,485`, is the fifth largest clone in the
experiment at 99 cells, and the 3′ channel cannot see it at all.** Not for want of reads: three
discovery clips of 44–49 bases end at exactly 5,676,485, the called junction base, with no
mismatches. All three align at **MAPQ 0**. The host sequence immediately 3′ of that junction is
repetitive, so a 44-base clip has nowhere unique to go, and the `MAPQ ≥ 30` filter — which is the
only thing standing between discovery and the genome's repeats — discards them. The genome-mapped
reads at the same junction carry 120–140 bases of host and land at MAPQ 255. Same locus, same
junction base, same cells; the difference is entirely how much host each read brought with it.

Across the whole 3′ channel, 86 of 974 discovery clips (8.8%) sit at MAPQ 0. That is the size of the
blind spot, and IS10 is what it was hiding.

### Site labels are pinned, not ranked

`IS01`–`IS15` are pinned to loci by [`metadata/integration_site_registry.csv`](../../metadata/integration_site_registry.csv),
and the table above is *sorted* by size without being *numbered* by it.

This is a correction, not a convenience. The labels used to be ranks, so when the genome-mapped
channel joined discovery and `chr9:53,079,916` overtook `chr13:83,681,311` on cell count, `IS01`
through `IS04` all moved — every sentence in this report that named a site silently came to mean a
different site. A rank is not an identity. The registry pins a locus to its number permanently, gives
a newly discovered locus the lowest number never yet used, and is tracked in git, unlike anything
under `output/`. Its first nine rows were seeded by hand with the numbering this report was already
written against, so `IS01`–`IS09` mean what they have always meant and the six sites the
genome-mapped channel added are `IS10`–`IS15`.

### Three sites the assignment step is forbidden to use

Three rows are held out of the mini-reference, and the table below marks them. They are shown rather
than quietly dropped, because a site discovery found and assignment was then not allowed to touch is
a different thing from a site that was never there.

Cell assignment works by matching clips against the flanks of the called sites (see the tier table
above), so a flank has to be distinctive enough to match *against*. A flank containing a long
homopolymer is not: it attracts clips that belong nowhere in particular. IS07 is held out for that.
IS14 and IS15 are held out for the other reason the gate exists — both sit at the cell floor with no
5′ junction to vouch for them, so there is nothing to distinguish them from the background they were
called out of.

None of the three reports zero cells any more, and the reason matters. The genome-mapped channel
assigns a cell by reading 120–140 bases of host at MAPQ 255, not by matching a short clip against a
flank, so the mini-reference gate has no purchase on it: IS07 keeps 3 cells, IS14 and IS15 keep 2
each. That is the right outcome rather than a leak — the hazard the gate exists to stop is a bad
flank *attracting* clips, and a channel that never consults the flank cannot be fooled by it — but it
does mean the gate no longer caps a site's count, only its assignment-tier count. A site whose flank
cannot support quantification can still accumulate cells here, and for IS07 all three of them sit in
the mCherry⁻ fractions, exactly where the argument below says a real site should not be.

```{r low-complexity}
# longest run of one base in each site's flank, the quantity the pipeline gates on
flank_fa <- file.path(sites_dir, "work", "site_flanks.fa")
kept     <- if (file.exists(flank_fa)) {
  sub("\\|.*", "", grep("^>", readLines(flank_fa), value = TRUE)) |> sub(pattern = "^>", replacement = "")
} else character(0)

sites |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, chrom, pos, cells,
                   `in the mini-reference` = ifelse(site_id %in% kept, "yes", "NO - gated")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(`in the mini-reference`, dplyr::desc(cells)) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 12)) |>
  DT::formatStyle("in the mini-reference", target = "row",
                  backgroundColor = DT::styleEqual("NO - gated", "#fde8e8"))
```

The homopolymer-gated site is `JH584304.1:35,417` (IS07), on an unplaced scaffold, whose flank
carries a **23-base homopolymer** against 5–6 for every other site. Three independent things said it
was not real before the gate existed:

- it had **zero** cells in both high-signal tubes while carrying 14 in the mCherry⁻ fractions — a
  real site appearing only where there is least vector is backwards. It still does: its three
  surviving cells are 2 in Rx_3 and 1 in Rx_7, and none anywhere else
- it has no 5′ junction, so the target-site duplication check cannot support it
- when the assignment threshold was lowered it gained **4.7×** more cells, against 1.6× for genuine
  sites: it was absorbing the extra sensitivity rather than benefiting from it

It therefore appears in the legend of every figure below with no points against it.

#### Why it is shown rather than dropped

The two stages ask different questions, and a site can pass one and fail the other without either
being a mistake.

| | asks | about | verdict on IS07 |
|---|---|---|---|
| discovery | does this ≥25 bp clip place uniquely in 2.7 Gb? | the **clip** | yes — 3 clips at MAPQ ≥ 30 |
| assignment | can this flank tell apart clips that belong to it from clips that do not? | the **locus** | no — the homopolymer |

The evidence is also partly independent: discovery's verdict comes from the read, assignment's from
the reference sequence around the site. So the gate never disputes that those three clips aligned
where they did. Its claim is narrower, and worth stating precisely: **this flank cannot support
quantification**. Not *no provirus is there* — unmeasurable, not false. The 4.7× inflation is that
claim measured directly.

That distinction decides what happens next. If a bulk integration-site assay on the same genomic DNA
ever gives an independently derived site list, `JH584304.1:35,417` is precisely the call it would
adjudicate.

Three reasons to leave the disagreement visible:

- **It localises the problem.** Agreement between the stages gives two kinds of support;
  disagreement says *where* the trouble is. Here it was the locus's sequence rather than the reads,
  which is what pointed at the homopolymer in the first place.
- **It measures a limit of the method.** The pipeline can call sites it cannot then quantify. A
  reader shown eight clean sites has no way to know that failure mode exists, or how one is handled.
- **It is a standing check on the gate.** `max_homopolymer` is a threshold chosen from a single
  example. Keeping the gated case in view means a future run producing a similar site that is *not*
  caught would be noticeable.

One detail sharpens all of this. Discovery's call was marginal to begin with: **3 clips, 3 cells,
against a floor of exactly 3** — and all three came from Rx_3 and Rx_7, the mCherry⁻ fractions, with
none from the two high-signal tubes. So this is not two confident stages contradicting each other.
It is a borderline call, admitted by a threshold with zero margin, that a second and independent
criterion then rejected, with the tube distribution agreeing. That is the system working rather than
an awkward edge case — and it is the clearest illustration of what the `≥3 cells` floor lets through
at its boundary.

```{r site-plot, fig.height=5}
cells_long <- sites %>%
  dplyr::select(site_id, gene, context, dplyr::starts_with("cells_")) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::starts_with("cells_"),
                      names_to = "tube", values_to = "cells",
                      names_prefix = "cells_") %>%
  dplyr::filter(cells > 0) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(label = ifelse(is.na(gene) | gene == "",
                               site_id, paste0(site_id, " · ", gene)))

ggplot(cells_long, aes(reorder(label, cells, sum), cells, fill = tube)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "cells carrying the junction", fill = "tube",
       title = "Integration sites by the number of cells supporting them")
```

## What the gene context tells us

Lentivirus does not integrate at random: it strongly prefers the bodies of actively transcribed
genes. That gives an internal control the analysis never assumed, so if the called sites are real they
should be enriched for intragenic positions in genes this tissue expresses.

```{r context}
sites %>%
  dplyr::count(context = sub(",.*", "", context), gene_type, name = "sites") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(sites)) %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

A site falling in an intergenic desert is not thereby wrong, but it is the kind of call to treat with
more caution — particularly at low cell counts.

**This is weaker evidence than it looks, and the obvious null is the wrong one.** Comparing 75%
intragenic against the genome's genic fraction would overstate the case, because a site can only be
*called* where a clip places uniquely, and unique sequence is itself concentrated in genes. The
filter that finds sites is correlated with the feature being tested.

The matched null draws 3,000 random genomic positions, puts a 40-mer from each through the same
`MAPQ >= 30` requirement a real clip must clear, and asks how many of the survivors are intragenic:

| | intragenic |
|---|---|
| mappability-matched random positions (n = 2,302) | **49.2%** |
| called sites (n = 8) | **75.0%** |
| | one-sided binomial **p = 0.135** |

The direction matches the literature and the effect may well be real, but at eight sites it does not
reach significance. Treat the integration preference as *consistent with* expectation rather than as
evidence for it. The sort agreement, replicate confinement and target-site duplication are
unaffected, and they are what the result rests on.

## The other end of the provirus

Everything above comes from one end of the provirus — reads running off its 3′ terminus. There is a
second, independent channel at the **5′** end, and it exists for the same reason the ψ artefact does:
reverse transcription makes both proviral LTRs identical and the contig keeps a single copy, so a
read crossing the **host → 5′ LTR** junction also lands on that copy, clipping host sequence to its
*left* instead of its right.

The anchor is contig 2736. The contig reads `…GGGGGG AC TGGAAGG…`, and integrase removes that `AC`
during 3′ processing, leaving the `TG` that partners the `CA` ending the contig at 3236 — the
canonical retroviral inverted repeat.

Unlike the 3′ end these anchors **smear**. The contig continues upstream of 2736, so host bases at the
clip's end that happen to match it are absorbed into the alignment by greedy extension and the
reported start slides left; a `GGGGGG` run at 2728–2733 makes this common. Anchoring on 2736 exactly
returns one clip; accepting a ten-base window and adding the absorbed bases back returns 150. The 3′
channel is immune because the contig simply stops at 3236, which is why 510 reads pile on one base
there.

### Target-site duplication

This is the strongest check in the report. Integrase cuts the two host strands with a **5 bp
stagger**, and repair fills the overhang, so those five bases are duplicated onto *both* flanks of
every provirus:

```
         ┌──────── 5 bp duplicated ────────┐
host ────┴──┬ CA ─── provirus ─── CA ┬─────┴──── host
            └─ 5′ junction           └─ 3′ junction
```

The two junction coordinates therefore differ by **4** (a 5 bp shared span). Two independent read
populations, from opposite ends of the provirus, must agree to the base. Nothing that merely
resembles a junction can produce that.

```{r tsd-table}
# One name per column, and the column set is checked rather than assumed: tsd_check() has gained
# columns twice (the duplicated span, then the observed-read fraction), and a colnames vector one
# shorter than the data is an error DT raises at render time, i.e. at the worst moment.
tsd_cols <- c(site_id = "site", chrom = "chrom", pos_3p = "3′ junction", pos_5p = "5′ junction",
              delta = "Δ", tsd = "verdict", tsd_seq = "duplicated span",
              tsd_obs = "span seen in 5′ reads", strand = "strand", strand_ok = "strand agrees",
              reads_5p = "5′ reads", cells_5p = "5′ cells")
stopifnot(setequal(names(tsd), names(tsd_cols)))

tsd |>
  dplyr::mutate(site_id = tidyr::replace_na(site_id, "—")) |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(names(tsd_cols))) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, colnames = unname(tsd_cols),
                options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 15, scrollX = TRUE)) |>
  DT::formatStyle("tsd", target = "row",
                  backgroundColor = DT::styleEqual("PASS", "#e8f5e9"))
```

Every site with enough 5′ reads to test passes at exactly 4 — IS01, IS03, IS04 and IS09 — and the
check goes further than the coordinate. A Δ of 4 can be manufactured by an off-by-one in either
channel, by a 0- versus 1-based slip, or by taking the wrong end of an alignment, and this analysis
has had all three. The duplicated **bases** cannot be manufactured that way: the two junctions must
share one five-base span of reference, and `span seen in 5′ reads` is the fraction of that cluster's
5′ reads that actually contain it. It is **1.00 at all four sites** — `GATTC`, `GTTCC`, `GAATA`,
`GTTCC` — so the reference and the reads agree base for base, and `strand agrees` confirms that the
sign of Δ matches the called strand in every case.

Two details about that table, both checked rather than assumed. `GTTCC` appears as the duplicated
span at two different sites, IS01 and IS09. The two values are read independently — each from its own
locus, `chr13:83,681,307-311` and `chr2:31,009,148-152`, by a separate reference lookup, and each
confirmed against that site's own 5′ reads — so it is a coincidence between two loci, not a
carry-over. A repeat among four 5-mers is a ~0.6% coincidence under uniform sampling and rather more
likely than that given integrase's target-site preference, so it needs no explanation beyond having
been verified.

And **the check cannot be run on IS10–IS15 at all.** The whole 5′ channel is 76 reads, which reach
only the largest sites; no 5′ cluster falls within 2 kb of any of the six new loci. Those sites are
therefore not *failing* the TSD test — they are outside its reach, and the TSD column is empty rather
than negative for them. For IS14 and IS15 that is the second independent thing missing, which is why
they are flagged `pooled_only`.

The rest of the table is as informative as the passes:

- **`no 3′ site nearby`** — a 5′ junction with no called site within 2 kb. These are candidate sites
  the 3′ channel missed, not errors. They are reported rather than dropped.
- **`distinct locus`** — a junction more than 50 bp from the nearest site. It is a separate feature
  that happens to lie nearby, *not* a failed duplication for that site. chr19:38,932,385 carries more
  reads than IS03's own 5′ junction while sitting 1.4 kb away; it is kept out of the arithmetic
  deliberately, and it is explained below — it is a spliced host exon, not a second integration.

### Seeing it

The duplication is easier to believe as geometry than as a number. Each panel is a window around one
site with both channels on a common axis anchored at the 3′ junction: 3′ clips above the line,
5′ clips below, each scaled within its own channel because the 3′ channel is up to a hundred times
deeper.

```{r junction-pileup, fig.height=8.5, fig.width=10}
tsd_band <- coverage |>
  dplyr::group_by(site_id) |>
  dplyr::filter(any(grepl("^5", channel))) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    lo = max(min(offset[grepl("^3", channel)]), min(offset[grepl("^5", channel)])),
    hi = min(max(offset[grepl("^3", channel)]), max(offset[grepl("^5", channel)])),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(bp = hi - lo + 1L, lab = paste0("TSD ", bp, " bp"))

coverage |>
  dplyr::group_by(site_id, channel) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel = depth / max(depth)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel = ifelse(grepl("^5", channel), -rel, rel)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = tsd_band, aes(xmin = lo - 0.5, xmax = hi + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = "#f0c200", alpha = 0.85, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_col(aes(offset, rel, fill = channel), width = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = tsd_band, aes(x = lo + bp / 2, y = 1.22, label = lab),
            size = 2.9, colour = "grey20", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ site_id, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = abs, limits = c(-1.1, 1.4)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-55, 55)) +
  labs(x = "offset from the 3′ junction (bp)", y = "coverage, scaled within channel", fill = NULL,
       title = "Chimeric read pile-up either side of each integration junction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

Three things are worth reading off it.

**Each channel stops where the provirus starts.** Neither spills across the junction, because a clip
is by construction the host half of a read whose other half aligned to the vector. The hard edge at
offset 0 is the provirus boundary, not a plotting limit.

**The orientation flips between sites.** Where the 3′ pile-up lies left of the junction the provirus
is on the minus strand, and right of it on the plus strand. The 5′ channel always takes the opposite
side, which is what two ends of one insert requires.

**They overlap by exactly 5 bases, every time.** That is the shaded band: the target-site duplication
drawn rather than asserted, the stagger integrase leaves, measured independently at four sites.
Sites with no 5′ reads show one channel and no band — missing evidence, not contrary evidence.

### What it has already caught

The check has already earned its place. It caught a coordinate bug in the 3′ channel — minus-strand
junctions were being reported about 48 bp from their true position, and worse, clips from one
junction were scattering far enough that clustering split them and dropped cells. Every filter in the
3′ channel was blind to it, because each fragment still clustered tightly on its own. Only the
disagreement with the 5′ end revealed it.

Two safeguards were added after that. The reported Δ is **signed**, because its sign is a free check
on the strand call — a plus-strand provirus has its 5′ junction above its 3′ junction and a
minus-strand one below — and `strand_ok` asserts the two agree. All four sites with both channels
pass. And `tsd_seq` is tested against **observed read sequence**, not only against coordinates: a
difference of 4 can be manufactured by an off-by-one in either channel, a 0- versus 1-based slip, or
the wrong end of an alignment, and this analysis has produced all three. The duplicated bases
themselves cannot be manufactured that way, and `tsd_obs` reports the fraction of each cluster's 5′
reads that physically contain the span. It is 1.00 at all four sites.

### A third channel: splicing into the provirus

Two 5′ junctions upstream of IS03 were unexplained for some time, at chr19:38,932,385 (32 reads in
14 cells) and 38,932,221 (1 read), 1,357 and 1,521 bp from the site. One GTF query and two base lookups settle the
larger one:

| test | sequence | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| is 38,932,385 an exon 3′ end? | annotated *Hells* exons `38932133-38932385`, `38932158-38932385` | yes |
| donor consensus after it | `38,932,384-389` = `GG` **`GT`** `AA` | canonical `GT` |
| acceptor consensus before the integration point | `38,933,737-742` = `TGTT` **`AG`** | canonical `AG` |

A canonical `GT`–`AG` intron running from a *Hells* exon donor into the provirus. For those 32 reads
this is not read-through at all but **splicing** from a host exon into the vector, which makes it a
third channel — and one carrying more reads than IS03's own read-in junction (32 against 27), though
at gene-level rather than base-pair resolution.

**The reads carry physical confirmation of the splice, and it was found by chasing what looked like
a bug.** 33 of the 76 placed 5′ hits end in a 4-base soft clip — `bwa` aligns the clip and then
refuses its last four bases. A constant 4-base tail next to a TSD test that expects Δ = 4 looks
exactly like a coordinate error, so it was run down. All 33 sit at the two spliced junctions
(`38,932,385` and `38,932,221`), and in every one the four refused bases are **`ATTC`** — the last
four bases of IS03's duplicated span `GATTC`, which lies **1,357 bp away** at the integration site.
The host sequence immediately after the exon is `GTAA`, the intron's donor, so `bwa` is right to stop
there and right to refuse `ATTC`: no contiguous alignment exists.

So the clip physically contains a *Hells* exon joined directly to the target-site duplication of the
provirus, with the intron absent. That is the splice, in the read, at base resolution — independent
of the GTF query and the consensus lookups above, which is what makes it worth the detour. It also
clears the absorbed-base repair in `read_five_prime_clips()`: the four bases are real host sequence
carried across the splice, not an over-extension. The pipeline correctly declines to call it a second
integration: `tsd_check()` labels anything beyond 50 bp a `distinct locus` rather than a failure of
the nearby site. The 1-read neighbour at 38,932,221 has no `GT` after it and remains unexplained.

## Sharing between tubes

Tubes that are different sorted fractions of the same animal should share clones; tubes from different
animals should not. A wild-type tube should show nothing at all, and whatever it does show sets the
cross-tube background — index hopping and ambient contamination — against which small sites in the
other tubes have to be judged.

```{r sharing, fig.height=5}
ggplot(cells_long, aes(tube, reorder(label, cells, sum), fill = cells)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = cells), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "firebrick", trans = "sqrt") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "cells",
       title = "Which tubes each site appears in")
```


# Cell-level clone labels

`cell_site_assignments.csv` is the table that matters downstream: one row per cell per site, which
joins onto the Seurat metadata and turns a genomic locus into a clone label.

The two compartments are embedded separately, so each keeps its own UMAP: the HSC panel comes from
`mpn_processed_hsc_fullcc` (tubes Rx_3, Rx_4, Rx_5) and the MNC panel from `mpn_processed_mnc` (Rx_6,
Rx_7, Rx_8). Both carry the `umap.nn` reduction. The extraction's `tube` and `barcode` concatenate to
exactly the Seurat cell name, so the join needs no barcode surgery.

```{r join-metadata}
#' Cell names, sort label and UMAP coordinates for one processed compartment.
#' Returns a small tibble, so the Seurat object can be dropped immediately.
cell_embedding <- function(srt, panel) {
  emb <- Seurat::Embeddings(srt, "umap.nn")
  tibble::tibble(
    cell        = colnames(srt),
    panel       = panel,
    tube        = as.character(srt$tube),
    sample_name = as.character(srt$sample.name),
    sample      = as.character(srt$sample.name.long),
    # the hashtag demultiplex call: which replicate mouse this cell came from. "multiplet" and
    # "negative" are failures of the call, not animals, and appear mostly before QC.
    replicate   = factor(as.character(srt$dm2_class),
                         levels = c("TotalSeq-B0301", "TotalSeq-B0302", "TotalSeq-B0303",
                                    "TotalSeq-B0304", "negative", "multiplet")),
    compartment = as.character(srt$compartment),
    pass_cell   = srt$pass_cell,
    UMAP_1      = emb[, 1],
    UMAP_2      = emb[, 2]
  )
}

# Read one at a time: literal tar_read() so tar_knitr_deps() registers both as dependencies of this
# report, and sequential so the two objects are never resident together.
hsc <- cell_embedding(tar_read(mpn_processed_hsc_fullcc), "HSC"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
mnc <- cell_embedding(tar_read(mpn_processed_mnc),        "MNC"); gc(verbose = FALSE)

embedding <- dplyr::bind_rows(hsc, mnc) %>%
  # A factor with all three levels, not a character: the wild-type samples contain no labelled cells,
  # so as a character the facet below would silently drop the column that matters most.
  dplyr::mutate(sorted = factor(
    dplyr::case_when(
      grepl("_positive$", sample) ~ "FACS mCherry+",
      grepl("_negative$", sample) ~ "FACS mCherry−",
      grepl("wildtype",   sample) ~ "wild-type (no vector)"),
    levels = c("FACS mCherry+", "FACS mCherry−", "wild-type (no vector)")))
rm(hsc, mnc); gc(verbose = FALSE)

# tube + barcode is the Seurat cell name, e.g. Rx_4 + AAACCAAAGAATCATC-1 -> Rx_4_AAACCAAAGAATCATC-1
labelled <- assign %>%
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(tube, "_", barcode)) %>%
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(embedding, -tube), by = "cell")

dplyr::tibble(
  metric = c("cell-site assignments in the table",
             "in a tube these two objects cover",
             "matched to a cell in them",
             "of those, cells passing QC",
             "distinct cells with a clone label"),
  value  = c(nrow(assign),
             sum(assign$tube %in% unique(embedding$tube)),
             nrow(labelled),
             sum(labelled$pass_cell, na.rm = TRUE),
             dplyr::n_distinct(labelled$cell))
) %>% DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

**Where the labelled cells go, since the pipeline's count and the figures' count differ and the
difference should be named rather than noticed.** The pipeline writes **1,222 assignments over 1,195
distinct cells**. Counted outside the Seurat objects, they sit in the tubes like this:

| tube | Rx_1 | Rx_2 | Rx_3 | Rx_4 | Rx_5 | Rx_6 | Rx_7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| labelled cells | 1 | 5 | 36 | 665 | 1 | 466 | 12 |

and reach the joined table above by one subtraction:

- **−5 or so** in the stroma tubes, Rx_1 and Rx_2. Those tubes are in neither embedded panel — the
  HSC panel is Rx_3/4/5 and the MNC panel Rx_6/7/8 — so their cells cannot join and drop out of
  every figure below. One of them is the Rx_1 wild-type cell discussed under Limitations.

There used to be a second subtraction, and it was a defect rather than a filter. 33 barcodes in the
cell table appeared in no demultiplexer output at all, and the reason turned out to be that **none of
them was a called cell**: the BAM carries error-corrected `CB` tags for droplets Cell Ranger did not
call, and this pipeline read those tags without checking. They were the ambient population arriving
in the cell table as cells — 2.8% of it. `read_called_barcodes()` now restricts cell evidence to
Cell Ranger's filtered barcode list, captured with the run in `work/called_barcodes.csv.gz`, and the
filter removed **34** barcodes on the current run. The clip and genomic tables deliberately keep
them, because the ambient rate above is computed from exactly those rows.

The `pass_cell` row in the table above is the last step, and only the render can produce it, because
`pass_cell` lives in the Seurat objects; everything above it is reproducible from the CSVs alone.

Two separate drops are expected. Assignments in tubes these objects do not cover — the stroma tubes —
fall out at the second row. The larger drop is at the third: the extraction uses every barcode Cell
Ranger corrected, which is a substantially bigger set than the cells that survived calling and QC.
The fourth row equals the third because these processed objects are already QC-filtered, so it is a
consistency check rather than a further filter.

## Do the labels land where the sort says they should?

An independent check that costs nothing. These cells were FACS-sorted on mCherry protein before
sequencing, and that sort knows nothing about soft-clipped reads. If the junctions are genuine vector
integrations, labelled cells should sit almost entirely in the mCherry⁺ fraction.

```{r sort-check}
labelled %>%
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell) %>%
  dplyr::count(sorted, name = "labelled cells") %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

A handful in the mCherry⁻ fraction is expected rather than alarming: the sort gates on protein, and a
transduced cell expressing below the gate still carries the provirus. The same cells drove the
false-negative discussion in the transgene-detection report.

## Where the clones sit on the UMAP

### Before QC filtering

The embedding used everywhere else in this report is built from cells that passed QC. It is worth
looking at the unfiltered one first, from `mpn_raw_processed_hsc` and `mpn_raw_processed_mnc`, for one
reason: a clone label is attached to a *barcode*, and the extraction never consulted the QC flags. If
labelled cells were concentrated in the part of the manifold that QC later removes — debris, dying
cells, ambient-heavy droplets — that would undercut the whole analysis.

```{r raw-embedding}
raw_hsc <- cell_embedding(tar_read(mpn_raw_processed_hsc), "HSC"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
raw_mnc <- cell_embedding(tar_read(mpn_raw_processed_mnc), "MNC"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
embedding_raw <- dplyr::bind_rows(raw_hsc, raw_mnc)
rm(raw_hsc, raw_mnc); gc(verbose = FALSE)

labelled_raw <- assign |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(tube, "_", barcode)) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(embedding_raw, -tube), by = "cell")
```

```{r umap-raw, fig.height=6, fig.width=11}
raw_umap <- function(panel_name) {
  bg <- dplyr::filter(embedding_raw, panel == panel_name)
  fg <- dplyr::filter(labelled_raw,  panel == panel_name)
  ggplot(bg, aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
    geom_point(colour = "grey88", size = 0.25, stroke = 0) +
    geom_point(data = fg, aes(colour = site_id), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.9) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = site_palette, drop = FALSE) +
    labs(title = panel_name, colour = "clone",
         subtitle = sprintf("%s barcodes before QC, %s carrying a detected integration site",
                            scales::comma(nrow(bg)), scales::comma(nrow(fg)))) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}

raw_umap("HSC") | raw_umap("MNC")
```

```{r raw-vs-clean}
labelled_raw |>
  dplyr::count(panel, pass_cell, name = "labelled barcodes") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = pass_cell, values_from = `labelled barcodes`,
                     values_fill = 0L, names_prefix = "pass_cell_") |>
  dplyr::mutate(`% kept by QC` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * pass_cell_TRUE /
                                           (pass_cell_TRUE + pass_cell_FALSE))) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

Labelled barcodes are spread across the manifold rather than piled into one corner, so the labels are
not an artefact of low-quality droplets. Their QC survival, though, does not simply track the overall
rate, and the two compartments disagree about the direction:

| | labelled barcodes kept | all barcodes kept |
|---|---|---|
| HSC | **82%** | 69% |
| MNC | **58%** | 68% |

In HSC, labelled barcodes are *enriched* for cells that pass. That is the expected direction and has
a mechanical explanation: detection requires capturing one of a few read-through molecules, which is
likelier in a deeply sequenced cell, and deeply sequenced cells also pass QC more often. Labelling is
partly a depth assay.

MNC runs the other way, modestly. I do not have an explanation for that, and with 128 labelled
barcodes it is not a large enough sample to pursue one. It is recorded rather than explained, and it
is worth remembering before treating HSC and MNC clone sizes as directly comparable — the two
compartments do not lose labelled cells at the same rate.

### After QC filtering

This is the embedding the rest of the report uses.

```{r umap-clones, fig.height=6, fig.width=11}
clone_umap <- function(panel_name) {
  bg  <- dplyr::filter(embedding, panel == panel_name, pass_cell)
  fg  <- dplyr::filter(labelled,  panel == panel_name, pass_cell)
  ggplot(bg, aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
    geom_point(colour = "grey88", size = 0.25, stroke = 0) +
    geom_point(data = fg, aes(colour = site_id), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.9) +
    # Set1 caps at 9 colours and there are 15 sites, so a qualitative ColorBrewer palette is out;
    # site_palette is glasbey, built above for exactly this reason
    scale_colour_manual(values = site_palette, drop = FALSE) +
    labs(title = panel_name, colour = "clone",
         subtitle = sprintf("%s cells, %s carrying a detected integration site",
                            scales::comma(nrow(bg)), scales::comma(nrow(fg)))) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}

clone_umap("HSC") | clone_umap("MNC")
```

Grey is every cell passing QC in that compartment; colour is the few hundred carrying a detected
junction. The sparseness is the point and is not evidence of rarity — detection needs a read-through
molecule to have been captured for that specific cell, so most members of a real clone carry no
label. Read the colours as a *sample* of each clone, not its extent.

## The same map, weighted by how well each cell is supported

Every coloured dot above is drawn identically, which overstates the weaker ones. Each assignment
rests on a different amount of evidence, and there are two measures of it that mean different things:

| measure | range here | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| **UMIs** | 1 (96%), 2 (11 cells), 3 (2 cells) | *independent molecules* — the honest measure |
| **reads** | 1–9 | sequencing depth on those molecules, mostly PCR duplicates |

The principled choice is UMIs, and it is nearly useless here: 310 of 323 assignments rest on a single
captured molecule. So size encodes **reads**, which at least varies, and a black ring marks the 13
cells with more than one UMI — the only ones whose evidence is genuinely independent.

```{r umap-confidence, fig.height=6, fig.width=11}
confidence_umap <- function(panel_name) {
  bg <- dplyr::filter(embedding, panel == panel_name, pass_cell)
  fg <- dplyr::filter(labelled,  panel == panel_name, pass_cell) |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(reads))      # large drawn first, so small stay visible on top
  ggplot(bg, aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
    geom_point(colour = "grey88", size = 0.25, stroke = 0) +
    # Two layers, and the no-border one uses stroke = 0 rather than a colour. Every other way of
    # saying "no border" fails: colour = NA, whether mapped or fixed, makes ggplot treat the row as
    # missing and drop the point at draw time, and "transparent" (= white at alpha 0) collides with
    # alpha=, which overwrites the alpha channel and leaves an opaque white ring. stroke = 0 gives
    # the border no width, so its colour never matters.
    geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(fg, umis < 2),
               aes(fill = site_id, size = reads),
               shape = 21, stroke = 0, alpha = 0.85) +
    geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(fg, umis >= 2),
               aes(fill = site_id, size = reads),
               shape = 21, colour = "black", stroke = 0.7, alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = site_palette, drop = FALSE) +
    # limits from the whole table, not the panel: otherwise each panel scales to its own maximum
    # (6 in HSC, 9 in MNC) and a dot of a given size would mean different things in the two
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.2, 5), breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 6, 9),
                          limits = range(labelled$reads)) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
    labs(title = panel_name, fill = "clone", size = "reads") +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}

confidence_umap("HSC") | confidence_umap("MNC")
```

```{r confidence-table}
labelled |>
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell) |>
  dplyr::mutate(support = dplyr::case_when(
    umis >= 2   ~ "2+ UMIs (independent molecules)",
    reads >= 3  ~ "1 UMI, 3+ reads",
    reads == 2  ~ "1 UMI, 2 reads",
    TRUE        ~ "1 UMI, 1 read (weakest)")) |>
  dplyr::count(panel, support, name = "cells") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = panel, values_from = cells, values_fill = 0L) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

The conclusion to draw from this figure is not that some dots are trustworthy and others are not. It
is that **per-cell confidence is uniformly low**, because a cell is labelled only when one of its rare
read-through molecules happened to be sequenced. The evidence for a clone is not in any single dot; it
is in the 109 independent cells that carry IS01. Confidence lives at the site level, which is what the
`≥3 cells and ≥3 UMIs` floor in the pipeline tests, and this plot is best read as a reminder that no
individual dot should be leaned on.

## Detected clones by replicate

Each tube pools several hashtagged mice, and `dm2_class` records which one a cell was called to. That
makes this the figure that decides whether the clones are what they appear to be. A lentiviral
integration site is created once, in one transduced cell, in one animal. **A genuine clone must
therefore sit inside a single replicate.** A site spread evenly across replicates is not a clone — it
is cross-contamination, ambient vector, or a demultiplexing failure.

Shown before and after QC filtering, for each compartment. The grey in each panel is that replicate's
own cells.

```{r replicate-umap-fn}
replicate_umap <- function(emb, lab, panel_name, subtitle) {
  bg <- dplyr::filter(emb, panel == panel_name, !is.na(replicate))
  fg <- dplyr::filter(lab, panel == panel_name, !is.na(replicate))
  ggplot(bg, aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
    geom_point(colour = "grey85", size = 0.18, stroke = 0) +
    geom_point(data = fg, aes(colour = site_id), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.9) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = site_palette, drop = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~ replicate, nrow = 1, drop = FALSE) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
    labs(title = panel_name, subtitle = subtitle, colour = "clone", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
}
```

```{r replicate-hsc, fig.height=3.2, fig.width=13}
replicate_umap(embedding_raw, labelled_raw, "HSC", "before QC filtering")
replicate_umap(dplyr::filter(embedding, pass_cell), dplyr::filter(labelled, pass_cell),
               "HSC", "after QC filtering")
```

```{r replicate-mnc, fig.height=3.2, fig.width=13}
replicate_umap(embedding_raw, labelled_raw, "MNC", "before QC filtering")
replicate_umap(dplyr::filter(embedding, pass_cell), dplyr::filter(labelled, pass_cell),
               "MNC", "after QC filtering")
```

```{r replicate-table}
dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(labelled_raw, stage = "before QC"),
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::filter(labelled, pass_cell), stage = "after QC")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(replicate)) |>
  dplyr::count(stage, panel, site_id, replicate, name = "cells") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = replicate, values_from = cells,
                     values_fill = 0L, names_prefix = "") |>
  dplyr::arrange(stage, panel, site_id) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, filter = "top",
                options = list(pageLength = 20, scrollX = TRUE))
```

Read the table rather than the figure for this one: the question is whether each row has its mass in a
single column. Where a site is confined to one replicate, it behaves like a clone. Where it is spread,
it does not, whatever its total cell count — and that is a check the site-level thresholds in the
pipeline cannot make, because they only count cells and UMIs.

## The same map, split by sample

Each compartment pools three samples, and they are not equivalent: one sorted mCherry⁺, one sorted
mCherry⁻, one wild-type. Pooling them hides the single most informative comparison, because the
wild-type samples are the assay's negative control and should be empty.

`sample.name` is one-to-one with the tube, so the six samples are exactly the six cells of this grid.
Faceting on the sort fraction rather than the name itself keeps each compartment in its own row — the
two UMAPs are separate embeddings and must not be drawn in each other's panels.

Each panel shows **that sample's own cells** in grey, with its detected clones highlighted on top. So
the grey is a result too, not just scenery: it is where that sample sits in the shared embedding, and
the three samples do not occupy it identically.

```{r umap-by-sample, fig.height=7, fig.width=12}
sample_key <- embedding %>%
  dplyr::distinct(panel, sorted, sample_name, tube) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(panel, sorted)

ggplot(dplyr::filter(labelled, pass_cell), aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
  # The grey keeps `sorted`, so each panel is that sample's own cells and nothing else.
  geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(embedding, pass_cell),
             colour = "grey80", size = 0.2, stroke = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = site_id), size = 1.6, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_palette, drop = FALSE) +
  # drop = FALSE keeps the wild-type column, which has no labelled cells and is the point
  facet_grid(panel ~ sorted, switch = "y", drop = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Detected clones by sample", colour = "clone", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0))
```

```{r sample-key}
labelled %>%
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell) %>%
  dplyr::count(panel, sorted, name = "labelled cells") %>%
  dplyr::right_join(sample_key, by = c("panel", "sorted")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(`labelled cells` = tidyr::replace_na(`labelled cells`, 0L)) %>%
  dplyr::select(sample = sample_name, tube, compartment = panel, sorted, `labelled cells`) %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

The wild-type columns are the result to check first. Those animals never received the vector, so a
clone label there would be an outright false positive — ambient contamination or index hopping — and
would put a number on the floor beneath every other panel. The mCherry⁻ columns are a different
matter: those cells failed a gate on *protein*, which is not the same as lacking the provirus, so a
label there is informative rather than wrong.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r umap-facet, fig.height=7.5, fig.width=12, results="asis"}
# One panel per clone, so sites with few cells are not hidden under the larger ones; one tab per
# compartment, the clones wrapped into rows of square panels so each UMAP keeps its shape (a single
# row of 15 squashed every panel to a narrow strip). The grey layer has no `site_id`, so ggplot
# repeats it in every panel.
clone_cols <- 5
for (cmp in levels(factor(embedding$panel))) {
  cat("### ", cmp, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(
    ggplot(dplyr::filter(labelled, pass_cell, panel == cmp), aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
      geom_point(data = dplyr::select(dplyr::filter(embedding, pass_cell, panel == cmp),
                                      UMAP_1, UMAP_2),
                 colour = "grey90", size = 0.15, stroke = 0) +
      geom_point(colour = "firebrick", size = 1.1) +
      facet_wrap(~ site_id, ncol = clone_cols, drop = FALSE) +
      labs(title = paste0("Each clone on its own panel: ", cmp), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
      theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
            panel.grid = element_blank(), aspect.ratio = 1)
  )
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

:::

The same clones, one tab each, with HSC and MNC side by side: where a clone sits in one
compartment against where it sits in the other.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r umap-facet-by-clone, fig.height=5, fig.width=10, results="asis"}
# Each compartment has its own embedding, so scales are free; the grey layer carries `panel`, so
# each side gets its own compartment's cells. drop = FALSE keeps a compartment with no cells of the
# clone as an empty map, which is itself the result.
clone_ids <- levels(factor(labelled$site_id))
bg_cells  <- dplyr::select(dplyr::filter(embedding, pass_cell), panel, UMAP_1, UMAP_2)
for (clone in clone_ids) {
  cells <- dplyr::filter(labelled, pass_cell, site_id == clone)
  n_by  <- table(factor(cells$panel, levels = levels(factor(bg_cells$panel))))
  cat("### ", clone, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(
    ggplot(cells, aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2)) +
      geom_point(data = bg_cells, colour = "grey90", size = 0.15, stroke = 0) +
      geom_point(colour = "firebrick", size = 1.3) +
      facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free", drop = FALSE,
                 labeller = labeller(panel = function(p) sprintf("%s (%d cells)", p, n_by[p]))) +
      labs(title = paste0("Clone ", clone, ": HSC and MNC"), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
      theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
            panel.grid = element_blank(), aspect.ratio = 1)
  )
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

:::

A clone confined to one region of the embedding would suggest its cells share a state; one scattered
across the map suggests the opposite. With these numbers, treat any apparent clustering cautiously —
a handful of cells will look clustered by chance on a map of tens of thousands.

## Clone sizes by compartment

```{r clone-sizes}
labelled %>%
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell) %>%
  dplyr::count(site_id, sorted, panel, name = "cells") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = panel, values_from = cells, values_fill = 0) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(total = rowSums(dplyr::pick(dplyr::where(is.numeric)))) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total)) %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 20, scrollX = TRUE))
```

Reading a clone present in both HSC and MNC as evidence of ongoing output from a labelled stem cell is
tempting, and it is the interesting hypothesis — but note the asymmetry in what the two fractions
sample, and that both are drawn from the same ambient pool, before leaning on it.

## Cells carrying more than one site

```{r ambiguous}
amb <- labelled %>%
  dplyr::filter(pass_cell) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(tube, barcode, n_sites_in_cell)

dplyr::count(amb, n_sites_in_cell, name = "cells") %>%
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t"))
```

These are flagged rather than resolved, deliberately. A cell showing two strong junctions is either a
genuine multi-copy integrant or a doublet, and no single cell tells you which. Treating them as
multi-copy clones would inflate clone counts; dropping them would deflate them. They are marked
