`ambiguous` so downstream analyses can make that choice explicitly.

Across all cells the two explanations make different predictions, so the comparison below is worth
making — but the denominator decides the answer, and the obvious choice for it is wrong.

Taking `n` to be the number of *labelled* barcodes builds the detection rate into the expectation
and all but guarantees the verdict "below chance". Under the same-clone hypothesis the right
denominator is the clone's **true size** `N`, which is far larger than the number of cells in which
a site was detected: cells showing both sites is then `|A| × |B| / N`. Inverting that is informative
in itself — 146 × 190 / 12 = 2,312 is the clone size in Rx_4 *if* IS01 and IS02 mark one clone, and
3,164 is the same figure for Rx_6, which are numbers to put next to the doublet explanation rather
than leave implicit.

The table therefore reports both denominators, and the conclusion follows the conservative one.

```{r cooccurrence}
cooccur <- function(tube_id) {
  d    <- dplyr::filter(assign, tube == tube_id)
  n    <- dplyr::n_distinct(d$barcode)
  sets <- split(d$barcode, droplevels(d$site_id))
  sets <- sets[lengths(sets) >= 3]
  ids  <- names(sets)
  if (length(ids) < 2) return(NULL)
  pairs <- utils::combn(ids, 2, simplify = FALSE)
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(pairs, function(p) {
    a <- unique(sets[[p[1]]]); b <- unique(sets[[p[2]]])
    obs <- length(intersect(a, b))
    dplyr::tibble(tube = tube_id, pair = paste(p, collapse = " + "),
                  cells_A = length(a), cells_B = length(b),
                  observed = obs,
                  # The denominator that builds in the detection rate, kept only for comparison.
                  exp_labelled = round(length(a) * length(b) / n, 1),
                  # Under the same-clone hypothesis, at a plausible true clone size.
                  exp_if_one_clone_2000 = round(length(a) * length(b) / 2000, 1),
                  # And the clone size that would be implied if the pair really were one clone.
                  N_implied = ifelse(obs > 0, round(length(a) * length(b) / obs), NA_integer_))
  }))
}

dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("Rx_4", "Rx_6"), cooccur)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(cells_A + cells_B)) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "tp", pageLength = 8))
```

Against the labelled-cell denominator every informative pair falls below expectation, which on its
own settles nothing: that denominator builds the detection rate into the expectation, and the zeros
are shared by both hypotheses — same-clone predicts ≈0.1 for a 45 × 5 pair and disjoint clones
predict 0, so their agreement discriminates nothing.

### The control that does discriminate: pairs from different mice

The hashtag demultiplex supplies a control the earlier analysis did not use. Every site is
mono-replicate, so **two sites in different mice cannot share a cell.** Any co-occurrence between
them is a doublet, an ambient pick-up, or a mistake. Splitting the pairs that way turns the doublet
explanation from an assumption into a measurement.

```{r cooccurrence-by-mouse}
# Which mouse each site belongs to: the dominant hashtag class, 96-100% of every site's cells.
site_replicate <- labelled |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^TotalSeq-B03", as.character(replicate))) |>
  dplyr::count(site_id, replicate) |>
  dplyr::group_by(site_id) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id = as.character(site_id), mouse = sub("^TotalSeq-", "", replicate))

pair_class <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("Rx_4", "Rx_6"), cooccur)) |>
  tidyr::separate(pair, into = c("A", "B"), sep = " [+] ", remove = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::rename(site_replicate, A = site_id, mouseA = mouse), by = "A") |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::rename(site_replicate, B = site_id, mouseB = mouse), by = "B") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mouseA), !is.na(mouseB)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(class = ifelse(mouseA == mouseB, "same mouse", "different mice"))

pair_class |>
  dplyr::group_by(tube, class) |>
  dplyr::summarise(pairs = dplyr::n(), observed = sum(observed),
                   `expected if independent` = round(sum(exp_labelled), 1),
                   `obs / exp` = round(sum(observed) / sum(exp_labelled), 4),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

A doublet process does not know which mouse a cell came from, so it would hit both classes at the
same rate. Apply the same-mouse rate to the cross-mouse pairs and it predicts **33.9** co-occurrences;
**one** was observed (Poisson *p* ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁴).

**The obvious objection to that, and why it does not hold here.** A droplet holding cells from two
mice carries two hashtags, which is exactly what a demultiplexer calls a doublet — so if such
droplets had been dropped before this test, cross-mouse pairs would have been stripped from the very
set the test runs on, along the exact axis of the comparison and in the direction of the conclusion.
That would be fatal. It is not what happened: **this test is run on every labelled barcode,
hashtag-multiplets included.** Of the 1,131 labelled cells in Rx_4 and Rx_6, 971 are called singlets,
**130 are called multiplets** and 30 have no call. Splitting the test by the demultiplexer's own
verdict shows where the one event lives (same minimum site size of three cells throughout, so the
first row is the table above pooled over both tubes):

| subset of barcodes | cells | cross-mouse obs / exp | same-mouse obs / exp |
|---|---|---|---|
| all labelled cells (what the test uses) | 1,131 | 1 / 263.5 | 26 / 202.1 |
| hashtag **singlets** only | 971 | 0 / 226.0 | 23 / 174.7 |
| hashtag **multiplets**, negatives, no call | 160 | 1 / 32.8 | 3 / 27.0 |

The single cross-mouse co-occurrence — Rx_4, IS02 + IS10, B0303 + B0304 — **is** a called multiplet,
precisely as a doublet should be: the demultiplexer caught it rather than hiding it. And in the
subset most enriched for doublets, cross-mouse co-occurrence is still **33-fold below independence**
rather than near it, while same-mouse co-occurrence in that same subset sits at the same ratio as
everywhere else. The depletion is not an artefact of demultiplexing.

**So doublets do not explain the co-occurrences, and the earlier claim that they could is withdrawn.**
Ambient goes with them: ambient RNA comes from the whole tube's soup, which carries every mouse's
clones in proportion to their abundance, so it too would produce cross-mouse pairs. One event in 263
expected is the measured ceiling on both mechanisms together. The reason both are so rare is worth
stating because it is not obvious: for a doublet to *show* two sites, **both** of its cells must be
detected, and detection is a few per cent per cell.

What is left is that sites **within one mouse share cells far above that floor**, which is what a
multi-copy founder looks like. Every one of the 26 co-occurrences is in B0303, and all six
co-occurring pairs are drawn from IS01, IS02, IS06 and IS08.

**Which expectation came from which model, because the two point opposite ways.** The 202.1 above is
`|A|·|B| / N_labelled`: the independence expectation *if every cell of every clone were detected*.
Same-mouse co-occurrence at 26 against that is running at an eighth of it — and read naively that
argues against sharing, since cells of a multi-copy founder carry both proviruses by construction.
It is not the right expectation. Under a shared founder the denominator is the clone's **true** size,
so the prediction is `|A|·|B| / N_true`, and 26 observed is then a statement about how much larger
`N_true` is than the detected count — the eight-fold shortfall *is* the detection rate. The
cross-mouse contrast is immune to this, because both classes use the same convention and the
comparison is between them, which is why the result rests on it.

### The discriminator that uses detection depth

Co-occurrence counts cannot separate "one clone, partly detected" from "two clones plus correlated
detection", because both are fitted by choosing a denominator. Detection *depth* can. If IS01 and
IS02 sit in one founder, every cell of it carries both and the only reason both are not seen is how
many junction molecules that cell yielded. So condition on that count:

```{r dose-response}
# P(cell carries both sites | how many junction molecules it yielded), against the prediction if the
# two sites were one clone: k molecules drawn from two proviruses with probability p and 1-p of
# landing at each, so P(both) = 1 - p^k - (1-p)^k. A cell with one molecule cannot show two sites,
# which the prediction accounts for rather than being confounded by.
mol <- assign |>
  dplyr::filter(tube %in% c("Rx_4", "Rx_6")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(m = umis_three + umis_genomic)
depth <- mol |>
  dplyr::group_by(tube, barcode) |>
  dplyr::summarise(k = sum(m), sites = list(as.character(site_id)), .groups = "drop")

curve_for <- function(a, b, label) {
  p <- sum(mol$m[mol$site_id == a]) / sum(mol$m[mol$site_id %in% c(a, b)])
  depth |>
    dplyr::mutate(hasA = purrr::map_lgl(sites, ~ a %in% .x),
                  hasB = purrr::map_lgl(sites, ~ b %in% .x)) |>
    dplyr::filter(hasA | hasB) |>
    dplyr::mutate(k = pmin(k, 4L)) |>
    dplyr::group_by(k) |>
    dplyr::summarise(cells = dplyr::n(), both = sum(hasA & hasB),
                     observed = round(mean(hasA & hasB), 3), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(pair = label,
                  `if one clone` = round(1 - p^k - (1 - p)^k, 3))
}

dplyr::bind_rows(
  curve_for("IS01", "IS02", "IS01 + IS02 — same mouse (B0303)"),
  curve_for("IS02", "IS04", "IS02 + IS04 — different mice (control)")) |>
  dplyr::select(pair, molecules = k, cells, both, observed, `if one clone`) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

| molecules in the cell | IS01 + IS02, same mouse | if one clone | IS02 + IS04, different mice |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 / 491 | 0.000 | 0 / 389 |
| 2 | **12 / 114 = 0.105** | 0.493 | 0 / 91 |
| 3 | **7 / 22 = 0.318** | 0.739 | 0 / 20 |
| 4+ | 1 / 8 = 0.125 | 0.864 | 0 / 8 |

**There is a dose–response, and the matched control is flat at zero.** Sharing rises with detection
depth for the same-mouse pair — 0, then 10.5%, then 31.8% — and stays at exactly zero for the
cross-mouse pair at every depth including the eight deepest cells. At matched depth `k = 2` the
contrast is 12 of 114 against 0 of 91, Fisher exact *p* = 0.0014. Doublets and correlated detection
do not produce a depth gradient in one pair and a flat zero in another; partial detection of a
shared founder does.

**But the gradient tops out around a quarter of what full sharing predicts** — 0.105 against 0.493
at `k = 2`, 0.318 against 0.739 at `k = 3`. Taken at face value that says roughly a quarter to a
third of these cells carry both proviruses and the rest carry one: a double-insertion sub-clone
inside B0303 rather than a single founder carrying everything. That also explains the inconsistent
implied sizes the pair-counting produced — IS01 + IS02 implying 2,312 cells against IS01 + IS06
implying 365 — which the previous draft could only record as a caveat.

**One piece of internal consistency, worth stating because the hypothesis has little else.** IS03 is
a B0303 site with 130 cells and it appears in **none** of the 26 co-occurrences. Under the
sub-clone reading that is exactly right: IS03 is an independent clone in the same mouse. Under a
doublet mechanism its absence would be unexplained, since doublets do not know which sites travel
together.

**Verdict.** Doublets and ambient are excluded as the dominant mechanism, by a control that
survives the one objection that would have killed it. A **double-insertion sub-clone inside B0303**,
carrying IS01 and IS02 in perhaps a quarter to a third of its cells, is the reading that fits both
the cross-mouse contrast and the depth gradient; IS03's absence from every co-occurrence is
consistent with it. The original "multi-copy founders are absent" was wrong, and the "undetermined"
that replaced it was too weak.

What is still open is the structure, not the existence: how many founders B0303 holds, whether IS06
and IS08 belong to the same sub-clone, and how much of the shortfall against full sharing is a real
sub-clone fraction rather than residual correlated detection. The `ambiguous` flag stays as it is so
downstream work can decide for itself.

What the data *does* settle is **replicate separation**, and the genome-mapped channel sharpened it
considerably. Every site is mono-replicate — the dominant hashtag class accounts for 96–100% of each
site's called cells — and the fifteen sites divide three ways:

| replicate | sites | labelled cells |
|---|---|---|
| B0303 | IS01, IS02, IS03, IS06, IS07, IS08, IS13 | 819 |
| B0304 | IS05, IS10, IS11, IS12, IS14, IS15 | 197 |
| B0301 | IS04, IS09 | 197 |
| B0302 | none | 0 |

Sites in different animals are necessarily distinct founders, whatever the within-replicate structure
proves to be. The change from the previous run is B0304: it had exactly one site, and now it has six,
headed by IS10 at 99 cells. The seven B0303 sites remain unresolved against each other.

#### The other instrument, and why it does not decide this

There is a second way to measure assignment error, and it is tempting because it runs on real reads
rather than decoys: every site belongs to exactly one mouse and every cell's hashtag names its mouse,
so **a clip assigned to a site in the wrong mouse is a detectable error**. It needs the hashtag calls,
which live in the targets store rather than the pipeline's outputs, so it is computed here:

```{r mono-replicate}
# Every assignment-tier match, with the mouse of its site and the mouse of its cell. A landing in
# the wrong mouse is an error that real reads can show, at every clip length.
mono <- clip_site_matches(file.path(sites_dir, "work", "all_clips.fa"),
                          file.path(sites_dir, "work", "site_flanks.fa"), min_len = 1L) |>
  dplyr::filter(assign_keep(clip_len, nm, budget)) |>
  dplyr::semi_join(dplyr::select(sites, site_id), by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(tube, "_", barcode)) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(site_replicate, site_id, site_mouse = mouse), by = "site_id") |>
  dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::transmute(embedding, cell,
                                     cell_mouse = sub("^TotalSeq-", "", as.character(replicate))),
                    by = "cell") |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^B03", cell_mouse)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cross = cell_mouse != site_mouse,
                band = cut(clip_len, c(0, 9, 14, 19, 29, Inf),
                           labels = c("6–9", "10–14", "15–19", "20–29", "30+")))

dplyr::bind_rows(
  mono |> dplyr::group_by(band) |> dplyr::summarise(molecules = dplyr::n(),
            `cross-mouse` = sum(cross), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(band = as.character(band)),
  dplyr::tibble(band = "pooled", molecules = nrow(mono), `cross-mouse` = sum(mono$cross))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rate = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * `cross-mouse` / molecules)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

It passes at the current floor and it is reported for that. **It cannot set the floor**, for two
reasons that are structural rather than fixable by more data.

It measures chance matching *plus* hashtag misassignment *plus* doublets. Four of the seven
cross-mouse landings sit at 23, 27 and 45 bases, where an exact positional match to the wrong flank
is not a coincidence, so the confound floor is **0.48%** against a 1% tolerance. And the resulting
power at the band that matters — 94 molecules at 6–9 bp — is not close to sufficient:

| if the true clip error were | power to detect it |
|---|---|
| 1% | **8%** |
| 2% | 20% |
| 5% | 62% |
| 10% | 93% |

So it can exclude an error rate above ~5% and cannot certify one below 1%, which is the only decision
a floor needs. The decoy flanks measure chance matching alone, and 100 of them can be cut against 94
real molecules, so they have the sample size this lacks. **Set the floor from decoys; read this curve
as a sanity check that happens to agree.** One detail worth recording either way: all seven
cross-mouse landings are on IS01 or IS02, the two largest clones, which is the prior-inflation
signature — ambiguous evidence drifting onto the biggest hypothesis — showing up even at the current
floor.


### Clone size: a detection rate that works, and a capture–recapture that cannot

The two channels read the same junctions through different reads, so the tempting argument writes
itself: a cell carrying a clone can be captured by either channel, the overlap between them measures
the capture probability, and Chapman's `(n₁+1)(n₂+1)/(m+1) − 1` turns that into the clone size
*including* the cells neither channel saw. `channel_capture_recapture.csv` carries that calculation,
and the estimate that replaces it.

```{r channel-overlap}
readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "channel_capture_recapture.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_id, detected, umis_per_cell = round(umis_per_cell, 2),
                   frac_one_umi = round(frac_one_umi, 2),
                   lambda = round(lambda, 2), detection = round(detection, 3), n_ztp,
                   n_three, n_genomic, m_both,
                   chapman = round(chapman), `± se` = round(chapman_se),
                   m_expected = round(m_exp_molecule, 1), ratio = round(m_ratio, 2)) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 15, scrollX = TRUE)) |>
  DT::formatStyle("chapman", color = "#999999")
```

It returns 650–950 cells for the four largest sites against 130–342 detected: the assay would be
seeing a third to a half of each clone. **That number has no referent in this design**, and the
reason is structural rather than a matter of bias.

**It is a partition, not two samples.** Lincoln–Petersen estimates a population from two independent
*samples* of it. These two channels are not two samples — they are a partition of one. Every junction
molecule belongs to exactly one channel, decided by where its fragment straddles the junction: more
vector than host and it is read against the contig, more host than vector and it is read against the
genome. Nothing is released and recaptured, so there is no capture probability to estimate, and
`n₁n₂/m` is not a biased estimate of the clone — it is a ratio of two halves of one draw. No
correction rescues a quantity that has nothing to refer to.

The molecule model makes that concrete and predicts the overlap, which is the useful thing a wrong
model can do. Which channel a junction read falls in is decided by where its fragment straddles the
junction — more vector than host and it reads against the contig, more host than vector and it reads
against the genome — and every read of one UMI is a duplicate of one fragment. **The draw happens
once per molecule, not once per read**, so a cell can appear in both channels only if it holds at
least two junction molecules. Between 73% and 100% of cells hold exactly one. `m` is therefore small
for a reason that has nothing to do with undetected cells, and a small `m` is precisely what inflates
`N̂`.

`m_expected` is that model's prediction with **no hidden population at all**: for a cell with `k`
molecules and a per-molecule probability `p` of landing in the 3′ channel, `P(both) = 1 − pᵏ −
(1−p)ᵏ`, summed over the cells actually in hand. Across the eleven sites with at least ten cells it
predicts 110 cells in both channels against 150 observed. The same calculation done on reads instead
of molecules predicts 430 — being wrong by a factor of three is what the molecule distinction is
worth, and why `cell_site_assignments.csv` carries `umis_three` and `umis_genomic` and not only the
read counts.

So the mechanism is real and large. An earlier version of this section then reported a 40-cell
excess of observed overlap over that prediction, `z = 6`, and attributed it to residual correlation in
capture. **That excess was an artefact of counting, and the diagnostic that found it is one query.**

Under the model a molecule has one anchor length and therefore falls in exactly one channel, so a
cell holding a single molecule cannot appear in both. Ask whether the cells counted in `m` really
hold two molecules:

| of the 150 cells counted in both channels | |
|---|---|
| share at least one UMI between the channels | **72 (48%)** |
| hold only **one** distinct molecule in total | **52 (35%)** |
| `m` recounted on genuinely distinct molecules | **83**, against 150 as counted |

73 of 1,434 molecules appear in both channels, so the split is **not a partition at the molecule
level** — which is the assumption every channel-overlap estimator rests on — and a third of the
apparent two-capture cells are one molecule counted twice. With `m` on distinct molecules the totals
read 83 observed against 109.8 predicted, where before they read 150 against 109.8. The prediction
sits between the two ways of counting, so the honest statement is that **the overlap is consistent
with the per-molecule model and the earlier excess is withdrawn**. `m_distinct` and
`cells_sharing_a_umi` are in the CSV so the arithmetic is inspectable.

The consequence for the estimator is sharper than the consequence for the model. Any λ derived from
the channel overlap inherits the inflated `m`: fitted on these data it exceeds the molecule-count λ
at every site where both are defined, by 1.17× to 2.22×, in exactly the direction double counting
predicts. **That estimator is therefore not used here.** The one below uses the molecule counts,
which do not require the partition to hold.

#### The estimate the section actually needs

The same molecule counts that invalidate the overlap support a different estimator, and this one does
have a referent. If a clone's cells each yield Poisson(λ) *detected* junction molecules, the cells
with zero are exactly the ones missing from the table, and the mean of the **zero-truncated**
distribution — `λ / (1 − e^−λ)` — identifies λ from the cells in hand. Then `1 − e^−λ` is a per-cell
detection rate and `detected / (1 − e^−λ)` a clone size. No second sample is required.

```{r detection-model}
readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "detection_model.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::transmute(site = site_id, detected = cells,
                   `molecules/cell` = round(mean_molecules, 2), λ = round(lambda, 2),
                   detection = round(detection, 3), `clone size` = clone_size,
                   `95% CI` = ifelse(is.na(clone_lo), NA_character_,
                                     sprintf("%d – %d", clone_lo, clone_hi)),
                   `obs 1 mol` = obs_1, `exp 1 mol` = round(exp_1),
                   `obs 2 mol` = obs_2, `exp 2 mol` = round(exp_2)) |>
  DT::datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", pageLength = 15, scrollX = TRUE))
```

**Read the top row and the bottom row together.** IS05 averages 2.63 molecules a cell and the
estimator returns 63 against 57 detected — 91% detection, tightly bounded, and the one case where
the method can see what it is doing. The nine sites at or below 1.09 molecules a cell get `NA`: at
exactly 1.00 the fit is degenerate, λ → 0 and the clone size goes to infinity, so the pipeline
declines rather than printing a number. **Those are not nine gaps to fill later** — for a 2-cell site
the correction would be meaningless against its own uncertainty.

**The Poisson fits, which was not expected.** 240 IS02 cells hold one molecule against 232 predicted
and 76 hold two against 85; IS01 gives 273 against 269 and 37 against 43. The plan anticipated
overdispersion and a negative-binomial refit, on the strength of 150 both-channel cells against a
predicted 110 — and that excess turned out to be the same molecule counted twice. With the counting
fixed there is nothing left to refit. (Do not read the fit from the variance-to-mean ratio: a
zero-truncated Poisson with small λ is underdispersed by construction, 0.41 at IS02 and 0.17 at IS01,
so comparing it to 1 suggests a problem that is not there.)

### Repertoire completeness: what fraction of the transduced population these sites account for

Detection-corrected clone sizes make a question answerable that sat open for several rounds, and the
denominator it needs was in hand all along — the mCherry⁺ cells **sequenced**, not the FACS record.

```{r completeness}
readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "repertoire_completeness.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `mCherry+ cells sequenced` = scales::comma(mcherry_cells_sequenced),
    sites, `labelled cells` = scales::comma(detected_cells),
    `floor (no model)` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * floor_share),
    `detection-corrected cells` = scales::comma(corrected_cells),
    `corrected share` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * corrected_share),
    `unaccounted` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * unaccounted_share),
    `sites using imputed detection` = sites_with_imputed_detection) |>
  t() |> as.data.frame() |> setNames("value") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Two numbers, reported together because they bracket the answer from opposite sides. **2.8% is a
floor that assumes nothing**: even at perfect detection the fifteen sites cannot account for less of
the mCherry⁺ population than the cells they already label. **6.7% is the detection-corrected
estimate**, and it inherits λ's uncertainty — nine of the fifteen sites have no estimable λ and are
corrected by the median of those that do, which is the weakest step in the calculation and is
exactly why the floor is printed beside it.

Either way the direction is not in doubt: **these fifteen sites are a small minority of the
transduced population**, and any statement about the clonal repertoire should say so.

#### Where the rest of the junctions are, since they are visible

That invites the obvious objection — if ~93% of mCherry⁺ cells belong to no called site, why are
there no junction reads from them? There are, and the clip table says what becomes of them.

```{r unassigned}
readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "unassigned_molecules.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::transmute(`what the molecule is` = class, molecules, cells,
                   `cells with no assignment at all` = cells_with_no_assignment) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The decisive split is between the last two rows. A molecule whose clip is long enough to place and
which still matches no called site is either **at a real locus that failed the cell floor** — 20
molecules at a handful of positions, each with one or two cells, every one below `min_cells = 3`,
one of them `chrX:100,691,113` which the target-site-duplication rescue identified and which was
never promoted to a site — or it is **unplaceable**, 59 molecules at MAPQ < 30 or unmapped, which is
the repetitive-flank blind spot the genome-mapped channel partly repairs.

So the repertoire missing *within this data* is a few micro-loci below the calling floor plus that
blind spot — **not** a large population of undetected clones leaving no trace. The two findings are
consistent: the unaccounted 93% are cells of clones whose proviruses never yielded a captured
junction molecule at all, which is what a per-cell detection rate of 26–52% implies, so they are
invisible here by construction rather than by oversight. That is also why this estimate needs no
posterior model to reach it.

Three routes now bear on the size of the two large B0303 clones, and they differ in what they
assume: the zero-truncated Poisson gives **660 and 1,154** from molecule counts alone, with bootstrap
intervals of 593–753 and 942–1,480; the co-occurrence inversion gives **2,312** on the assumption
that IS01 and IS02 share a founder; and Chapman gives 648 and 948 from a design that cannot support
it. The first is the one to quote — it has a referent, an interval, and a fit check that passes.
All three agree the answer is **order 10³ against 318 and 342 detected**, and the co-occurrence
figure being the highest is consistent with its own assumption: if the two sites are one clone, its
size is the sum of what each sees, not either alone.

# Limitations

**Only intact proviruses are visible.** The junction filter requires a clean processed `CA`. Integrants
with deleted or rearranged LTR ends present no such junction and are invisible here. For clonality
that is arguably a feature, but it means site counts are a floor, not a census.

**The junction position is tied to the contig boundary.** 3236 is the last base of *this* contig. If
the cassette is ever re-cut with a different 3′ boundary, the filter position must move with it; the
constant lives in `scripts/slurm/analysis/integration-sites.sh`.

**Detection is read-through-limited, so absence is weak evidence.** A cell is labelled only if one of
its few read-through molecules happened to be captured and sequenced. Most cells in a real clone carry
no label. Clone *sizes* here are therefore samples, not counts, and comparing them across tubes
assumes comparable depth.

**Small sites sit near the background, and the wild-type tubes do not bound all of it.** A wild-type
tube bounds *cross-tube* error — index hopping and carry-over — and nothing else. It cannot bound
within-tube ambient, where every lysed mCherry⁺ cell sheds vector RNA into the shared soup. That is
measured separately from sub-threshold droplets, computed each run across both channels:

```{r ambient}
readr::read_csv(file.path(sites_dir, "ambient_rate.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(junction_barcodes >= 10) |>
  dplyr::transmute(tube, `junction-bearing barcodes` = junction_barcodes,
                   `of those, a called cell` = in_called_cells,
                   `not a cell` = not_cells,
                   `ambient share` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ambient_share),
                   `rate per called cell` = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * rate_per_cell),
                   `rate per empty droplet` = sprintf("%.1e", rate_per_empty),
                   `ratio` = scales::comma(round(ratio))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The comparison that makes the number mean something is the last column: a junction in one of 2.5
million empty droplets and a junction in one of 20,000 cells are different events, and per droplet
the signal is three to four orders of magnitude stronger in cells. These are also exactly the
barcodes the called-cell filter removes from the cell table — the filter is applied where cells are
counted and **not** to the clip and genomic tables, because this measurement is computed from the
rows it removes.

Folding in the genome-mapped channel was a check on this in its own right: it raised the
junction-bearing barcode count substantially and left the non-cell count unchanged. The new channel
added signal without adding ambient, which is what should happen if the extra reads are real
junctions rather than background — a doubling of a background-driven signal would have doubled its
background with it. Scaled by the depth difference between a cell and an empty droplet — the one
multiplier not measured here — this is of order 1–2% of labelled cells, consistent with the doublet
rate. Scaled by the depth difference between a cell and an empty droplet — the one multiplier not
measured here — that is of order 1–2% of labelled cells, consistent with the doublet rate.

The assignment tier's own error rate is now measured rather than argued, by **decoy flanks**: 100
flanks cut from random matched positions and carried through the identical positional test. They
return zero hits at every clip length from 10 bp up, which also audits the anchoring, since a decoy
has no junction and any hit passing it would mean the test is mis-implemented. Below 10 bp they
return 2, which is what set `min_assign`.

**The genome-mapped channel needed its own decoy, and it is a different decoy.** The flank decoys
bound assignment and say nothing about the channel that now calls four sites on its own and carries
IS10's 99 cells. That channel's claim is narrower: a read the aligner placed at MAPQ 255, whose
soft-clipped end matches the last 13 bases of the provirus terminus within the absorption window, is
a junction read. `genomic_decoy_rate()` tests how often that is true of a terminus that cannot be
there — the same 13 bases **permuted to the same composition**, which matters, because the real
13-mer `AAAATCTCTAGCA` carries six adenines and a permutation of the whole 18-base terminus leaves
only three. A-rich *k*-mers are commoner in a mammalian genome, so a composition-mismatched decoy
understates the rate in the direction that flatters the channel.

On chr19 in Rx_4 — 27.6M alignments, a slice that contains a real site with 29 reads —
`CCTACAAAGTTAA` returns **zero hits**. Nothing else on that chromosome in that tube looks like a
junction once the terminus is scrambled. Stated as a bound rather than as a zero: 0 observed puts a
95% Poisson ceiling of 3 events on that slice, against 29 real.

**The genome-wide pass has now run** (job 35768797, 2 h 00 m, all eight tubes), and the answer is
not zero:

| tube | Rx_1 | Rx_2 | Rx_3 | Rx_4 | Rx_5 | Rx_6 | Rx_7 | Rx_8 | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real reads | 0 | 12 | 47 | 800 | 1 | 537 | 25 | 0 | **1,422** |
| decoy reads | 0 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 5 | **15** |
| decoy positions | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 2 | 9 |

**1.1% of reads, and no callable site.** The 15 decoy reads scatter over 7 positions across 8 tubes —
at most a few reads at any one of them — while the 1,422 real reads concentrate at 47 positions, 800
of them at 16 positions in Rx_4 alone. A site needs `min_cells` distinct cells and `min_umis`
molecules at one base, and nothing in the decoy output approaches that. So the error rate to quote is
**1.1% at the read level and zero at the site level**, which is the level the site list is built at.

Two details worth keeping. **Rx_8 is the sharpest result in the table**: a wild-type tube, zero real
reads, and 5 decoy reads — so in material with no provirus at all, the real 13-mer finds nothing and
a composition-matched random one finds five. The real terminus is not merely better than chance here,
it is cleanly separated from it. And at the cell level 1.1% of 1,396 folded-in reads is roughly 15
reads, so of 1,195 labelled cells perhaps 15 could carry a spurious label — the same order as the
ambient and doublet rates, and not concentrated anywhere.

One limitation of this run, for whoever tightens it: `genomic_decoy_rate()` stores counts per tube,
not cells per decoy position, so "no callable site" is inferred from reads-per-position rather than
measured against the floor directly. That is the next thing to add if the bound ever needs to be
airtight.

It is a separate job rather than a stage of the main one because it costs what the genomic scan
costs, and a control must not sit on the critical path of a run someone is waiting for. It reads the
real counts from the genomic stage's cache instead of rescanning for them, which is the difference
between ~1 h 50 m and ~3 h 30 m.

The `≥3 cells and ≥3 UMIs` threshold remains the one genuinely arbitrary parameter in the chain. It
is also now demonstrably costing real sites: chrX:100,691,113 sat at 2 cells in the 3′ channel and
was recovered only by searching the single position its 5′ partner predicts.

**Per-clone detection is not uniform, so λ differs by site.** Vector expression per cell spans about
sevenfold across clones — median UMIs on the reporter contig run from 1 at IS03 and 3 at IS04 to 6 at
IS02 and 7 at IS05, with IS04 at roughly half of IS01 and IS02 combined (Wilcoxon *p* = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵).
This is direct evidence that position effects operate at these loci, and it means a per-site
detection rate assumed constant is misspecified — which matters for every clone-size statement.
Separately, read-through termination is multi-site: the vector-portion length distribution at IS02
shows at least three over-represented positions at molecule level (reads per UMI is flat at ~1.5
across it), so a λ built on a single termination site is also misspecified.

**Leakage into the mCherry⁻ tubes was reported here as animal-structured. On the proper
denominator it is not, and the correction is instructive.** The figures were B0304 14.0% of its
labelled cells in the mCherry⁻ tubes, against 3.6% for B0301 and 0.2% for B0303 — a seventy-fold
spread. Those numbers are arithmetically correct and they measure the wrong thing: they are the
*composition* of each mouse's labelled cells, and composition follows where that mouse's cells were
sorted.

```{r leakage-rates}
# Per-mouse, per-sort-fraction cell counts, from the hashtag call. The denominator is the only thing
# that makes the labelled counts comparable, and it is the quantity the metadata queries asked for.
sort_of <- function(tb) ifelse(tb %in% c("Rx_4", "Rx_6"), "mCherry+", "mCherry−")
mouse_cells <- embedding |>
  dplyr::filter(tube %in% c("Rx_3", "Rx_4", "Rx_6", "Rx_7"),
                grepl("^TotalSeq-B03", as.character(replicate))) |>
  dplyr::transmute(cell, tube, mouse = sub("^TotalSeq-", "", replicate), sort = sort_of(tube))

dplyr::left_join(
  dplyr::count(mouse_cells, mouse, sort, name = "cells"),
  labelled |>
    dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(mouse_cells, cell, mouse), by = "cell") |>
    dplyr::distinct(cell, mouse, tube) |>
    dplyr::mutate(sort = sort_of(tube)) |>
    dplyr::count(mouse, sort, name = "labelled"),
  by = c("mouse", "sort")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(labelled = tidyr::replace_na(labelled, 0L),
                `rate` = sprintf("%.3f%%", 100 * labelled / cells)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

B0304 has **92.0%** of its cells in the mCherry⁻ fraction — 20,817 of 22,632 — against 33.7% for
B0301 and 35.6% for B0303. Divide by that and the picture changes completely. (The figures below are
counted over every barcode the demultiplexer called; the table above recounts over this report's
embedding, so the two differ by whatever QC dropped. The ratios are not sensitive to that.)

| mouse | cells, mCherry⁺ | cells, mCherry⁻ | rate, mCherry⁺ | rate, mCherry⁻ | ⁻ as % of ⁺ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B0301 | 18,122 | 9,217 | 0.94% | 0.054% | **5.8%** |
| B0303 | 17,557 | 9,724 | 3.74% | 0.103% | **2.7%** |
| B0304 | 1,815 | 20,817 | 7.93% | 0.130% | **1.6%** |

The per-cell detection rate in the mCherry⁻ fraction spans 0.054% to 0.130% — a factor of 2.4, not
70 — and measured against each mouse's *own* mCherry⁺ rate, B0304 leaks the **least** of the three.
The earlier conclusion is withdrawn in both of its versions: it is not B0301 and it is not B0304.

This is the second time in this report that a composition has been mistaken for a rate, the first
being the labelled-cell denominator in the co-occurrence test. Both times the error produced a
large, clean-looking number pointing at a real-sounding conclusion. The guard is mechanical: **never
divide labelled cells by labelled cells.**

**What is left, and it is the more interesting finding.** B0304's cells are 92% mCherry⁻ while the
other two mice are near a third, and its mCherry⁺ cells carry the highest detection rate of any
mouse at 7.93%. That is a statement about the animal — engraftment, sorting, or vector expression —
and not about any integration site. It is the same phenomenon as the IS05 question below, in the
same mouse, and the two should be treated as one open item.

**IS10 follows from that, and nothing should be read into its mCherry⁻ fraction.** IS10 is a B0304
clone — 87 of 87 singlet-called cells — and its 26% mCherry⁻ fraction is its mouse's sorting
composition, not a property of the locus. Per cell it runs at 0.125% in the negative fraction
against 4.02% in the positive, a ratio of 3.1% against B0304's 1.6% overall: the same order, nothing
anomalous. **No silencing or position-effect claim should be built on IS10.**

**The 5′ channel advertises a 10 bp floor it does not have.** `classify_five_prime_clips()` sorts
5′ clips into a discovery tier at `min_discovery` (25 bp) and an assignment tier at `min_assign`
(10 bp), but only the discovery tier is ever written: `write_clip_fasta(five, "discovery", …)`. The
assignment tier is computed, counted in the waterfall, and then dropped. `five_prime.fa` contains no
clip shorter than 25 bases, which confirms it. This is the same family as `-T 30` and `-T 12` — a
threshold that reads as active and is not — except that here nothing silently discards the reads
downstream; they are never sent downstream at all.

The gain being left on the table is real but modest: those clips could be matched against the
mini-reference by the same exact positional test the 3′ assignment tier uses, since the flanks are
cut ±200 bp around the 3′ junction and so contain the 5′ junction four bases away. It is a design
change rather than a fix, so it is recorded rather than made. Note also that the 5′ discovery clips
that *are* sent place poorly — 44% of the 25–34 bp band reaches MAPQ ≥ 30, 54% of 35–49 — so this
channel sits in the same MAPQ-0 blind spot as the 3′ one.

**The 20 bp clustering window is not hiding junction-base scatter.** Reads are merged into sites
within `cluster_window = 20`, which could in principle absorb a spread of nearby junction positions
into one call and make a fuzzy site look exact. It does not: of the 1,396 genome-mapped reads that
fall inside a called site, **every one sits at offset exactly 0** from that site's junction base — one
distinct position per site, at all fifteen. The window could be set to 1 and nothing in this channel
would change. Integration is a point event and these reads resolve it to the base.

**Clip length biases which loci are findable, and that bias is now measured rather than asserted.** A
junction whose flanking host sequence is repetitive yields clips that align at MAPQ 0 and is silently
lost: 86 of 974 discovery clips (8.8%) sit at MAPQ 0. IS10 is what that was hiding — a 99-cell clone
whose three 3′ clips end on the junction base exactly and are all unplaceable. The genome-mapped
channel largely repairs this, because 120–140 bases of host place where 44 do not, which is why it
finds four sites the 3′ channel cannot and misses none that it can. What remains is that sites are
still enriched for integrations into sequence unique *at 130 bp* — which is also where genes are,
partly confounding the intragenic enrichment used above as a sanity check.

**A replicate's absence from a compartment may be sampling, not biology.** B0304 contributes 1,399
cells to Rx_4 but only **108** to Rx_6 after QC (1,614 and 201 before it — the counts in the
leakage table above are pre-QC, and the argument here uses the post-QC ones because the detection
rate it multiplies is also post-QC). At IS05's detection rate in Rx_4 (2.64%) that predicts ≈2.9
labelled cells in Rx_6 against 0 observed, *p* ≈ 0.055 — so the apparent "IS05 is HSC-only" pattern is
not supported, and no lineage claim should be built on it. The same caution now has a second
instance: IS05 is one of six B0304 sites rather than that animal's only clone, and IS10, IS11, IS12,
IS14 and IS15 are all sampled from the 1,815 mCherry⁺ cells B0304 contributes against 17,557 for
B0303. **Every B0304 result in this report rests on a tenth of the cells the other animals supply.** B0302 likewise has only 215 cells in Rx_4,
so its zero labelled cells bound within-tube ambient only weakly (<~1.4%), far less tightly than the
empty-droplet measurement above. B0304's hashtag-to-animal mapping used to be the one that could not be
cross-checked by shared clones between compartments, because its only clone was the one missing from
MNC. IS10 closes that: it carries 69 cells in Rx_4 and 4 in Rx_6, so B0304 now has a clone on both
sides of the compartment split.

Even with more cells, RNA could not settle it. If the IS05 provirus sits in a locus that
heterochromatinises on differentiation, the promoter silences, read-through stops, and this pattern
appears with no lineage difference at all — and a silenced provirus is equally absent from the
mCherry⁻ tube. Only DNA distinguishes the two: a bulk integration-site assay on sorted mature B0304
cells, asking whether the IS05 junction is present in genomic DNA. Present in DNA and absent in RNA
means silencing; absent in DNA means genuinely no mature output.

**The ~50 bp clip edge is real but unexplained.** Both channels taper off sharply above ~50 bp of
clipped sequence, with maxima of 62 (host clip) and 69 (vector clip). It is *not*
`outFilterMatchNminOverLread`: chr19 alone holds 30,889 reads of exactly 150 bp with clips ≥ 60 and
matched fractions down to 30–39%, so no 0.66 filter is in force. The implied gap is roughly 70–87
bases of anchor. The reads are absent rather than mis-placed — every read overlapping a junction is
MAPQ 255 with no supplementary, secondary or low-MAPQ population, on both plus- and minus-strand
sites — so there is no hidden yield there, but the cause is not established.

**These reads are counted as host-gene expression — at four sites of the fifteen, and the rule for
which is exact.** A genome-mapped junction read is an ordinary alignment to the host gene as far as
Cell Ranger is concerned: it carries `GN:Z:<host gene>` and `xf:i:25`, and bit 8 of `xf` is the flag
that makes a read a UMI count. So for an affected site the carrying cells gain host-gene UMIs that
are really vector transcript, in exactly the cells a cis-effect test would compare.

It needs **two** conditions, and the second keeps it off most sites. The read has to land inside the
gene, and it has to be in the gene's own orientation — an antisense read is tagged with the gene but
not counted. An earlier draft of this paragraph cited "177 spurious *Ddx10* UMIs in Rx_4"; that was
wrong, because IS02's provirus is antisense to *Ddx10* and none of those reads is counted. The
prediction was tested against the count matrix at six sites and it holds at all six:

| site | host gene | orientation | junction share of carriers' host-gene UMIs |
|---|---|---|---|
| IS10 | *Gm35330* | same sense | **23.5%** |
| IS04 | *Abhd17c* | same sense | **20.9%** |
| IS11 | *Stau2* | same sense | **12.1%** |
| IS03 | *Hells* | same sense | 2.3% |
| IS02 | *Ddx10* | antisense | 0.4% |
| IS01 | *Mef2c* | antisense | 0.0% |
| IS09 | *Fnbp1* | antisense | 0.0% |

`integration_sites.csv` carries this as `cis_confound`, true for **IS03, IS04, IS10 and IS11**. For
those four, any cis-effect test must drop UMIs whose reads contain the provirus terminus before
comparing anything; for the other eleven the question does not arise. IS03's share is small only
because *Hells* is highly expressed, not because the mechanism is weaker there.

**What this measurement is not.** Carrying cells do show more host-gene signal than other cells —
2.5× for *Hells*, 4.0× for *Stau2* — and removing the junction UMIs does not remove that. It is not
evidence of a cis-effect either, because "other cells" here is every other cell in the tube, which
mixes cell type with clone identity: a clone is a lineage, and its host gene may simply be a gene
that lineage expresses. The confound is now quantified and removable; the cis-effect question is
untouched and needs a matched comparison.
